Apparently everyone misses the "OG Money Twitter" days so I'm starting a thread of pure high-level online marketing tips that I'll be adding to throughout the day.

Enjoy:  When you're trying to drive real ROI with organic traffic (especially video-focused platforms like YouTube and TikTok), you need to put yourself in the shoes of the platform.

With something like paid Facebook ads, the "win-win" is pretty clear: You pay them for their advertising space, and in return they show your content to your potential customers. They spend billions of $ a year aggregating data, so you can have the absolute best results possible. It is called an "auction" for a reason – the more you spend, the more they'll distribute your content.  But what about organic platforms that you don't pay for? What are you going to give these platforms in return for showing customers your content?  Well, think to the example above – these platforms get paid through advertisments. The more advertising revenue they can make, the better.   So, if you're not going to pay them directly, you need to help them generate as much revenue as possible from people who ARE paying them.  This is where the idea of "retention" comes in. If your organic content makes viewers stay on the platform 2x as long, that's 2x more advertising space they can sell, which means it's in the PLATFORMS' best interest to show your content to more people.   This is why the meta on YouTube right now is linking other videos on your channel in your video description.  Think back to when everyone started only posting 10+ minute videos. Some people were adding blank space to the end just to get it over the 10min mark. There was a direct ROI in ad revenue.   YouTube is the strongest example of this but it goes for other platforms. This is why TikTok creators will do "Part 1" of a video, cut it off, then post Part 2, Part 3 etc.   Remember you're not just "posting content' you're directly contributing to an advertising/data monopoly. You need to pay the piper    Market awareness is way up in bizop. CPCs are 2-3x higher than they were a few years ago. Everyone is competing for the same limited space with the same angles. You can't "trick" the market anymore. Nobody is getting on a webinar without EXPECTING there to be a pitch. If you run whitehat live webinars, you'll see comments flooding with "where's the pitch course scammer!" If you're selling high awareness B2B, just drop the gimmicks altogether. Go extremely mechanistic, explain why YOUR solution is better, newer, safer, easier than your competitors. Explain what is currently happening in the world, politics, economy, technology, social trends etc. that enables your solution. Study old Agora angles, it was usually "This \[thing happening in the world] is letting people like you achieve \[outcome]" If you're selling a high ticket sales program, it's unlikely you're getting a flood of people who have NEVER heard of HTS before. So you have two options: a) Create a new angle altogether and go low awareness. Drop the HTS. There was a program (forget which one) that framed it as becoming a "digital customer service representative" where you helped potential customers understand the program, get the support they need, collect payments and onboard them into the community
b) Create a new unique mechanism that beats everything else. Why is yours fundamentally different than the competition? Why did the programs they already purchase not work for them?\
Market awareness part 2.    If selling B2C or 0-1 bizop, again just assume most of your buyers have gone through some sort of make money online funnel and don't try to trick them.    The main focus here is congruency and HONESTY.   The reason everyone's moving away from opt ins on BAC funnels is the same reason as the last tweet – they know you're not giving them a "free training" that "reveals" their secret. You're just collecting their email, sending them to a VSL and hammering them with emails.   Even if they don't know this directly from experience, they have suspision you're selling them something.   If you want them to book a call, let them book a call. Just put the calendar right underneath the VSL. Or have a button that just says "Click Here To Apply ->" that takes them right to the app.\
The best "retargetting" you can do is just being the person they want to buy from. This means having a brand. Whether that's with a big organic following, or a shit ton of retargetting ads When you're doing a typical opt-in -> book a call -> email follow ups to get them to book, all you're REALLY doing is getting the people who were 70% of the way to booking but didn't over the edge.

If someone was NOT interested in booking (or purchasing) because you fundamentally didn't get them to trust you, or explain why your solution was right for them well enough, a 5 day email sequence is NOT going to suddenly shift their entire belief structure.

Sales cycles are long. It's a barbell theory – either people are already mentally bought in and need follow ups to just take the action, or they're NOT bought in and require a LOT more time spent with you (content)

Do you think people are buying from Brez because he has an extremely dialled follow-up sequence, or because he's fucking EVERYWHERE and is top of mind 24/7 for his target audience?\
Follow up to the above: you can run retargetting ads using your best performing organic content for DIRT cheap. Facebook knows who to show it to (obviously) and they likely just need to trust you more, so don't just hammer them with sales copy but actually NURTURE them\
Maybe the most important one:     ACTUALLY put yourself into your buyers' shoes. Most never do this. They just run copy angles that they "know works" and never ACTUALLY remove their personal bias.

```
 Think of the last time YOU made a 5-figure investment. Was it REALLY because of a razor sharp direct response campaign? Or did you just SEE the person for months, consume a lot of their content, hear other people say "yeah he's the best" etc.
 
 What % of Jeremy Haynes' mastermind customers bought DIRECTLY because of an ad campaign? How many of them were TRUE cold prospects? I'd best majority are in there because it's just KNOWN that that's where you go to get the best info. It is a ripple effect of social proof that nurtures you even when you're not directly consuming activation material              
```

Spaces that were saturated 3-4 years ago are basically blue oceans again when everyone jumped ship to make money online/SaaS/AI etc.       Iman was teaching Facebook ads for local businesses and it got giga saturated. Now everyone's just trying to be a growth operator for growth operators.

```
   If you can actually drive traffic, you can pitch law firms and doctors offices on 5x the retainers you can for a 17 year old selling ecom automation                
```

90% of the BIGGEST levers you can pull to increase ROAS on your ads are NOT in the ads manager.         There are baseline benchmark metrics everybody's basically hitting. If you are running good ads to a good offer, it's unlikely your ad metrics are going to be SIGNIFICANTLY different from competitors of your size. Lots of nuance here obviously but the point stands

```
     So, the absolute BIGGEST lever you can pull is LTV, and 7 day cash collected. This was basically the entire point of Hormozi's latest launch.
     
     Again, assuming you're running a decently optimized campaign, slashing your CPA in 1/2 by tweaking your ads is SIGNIFICANTLY more difficult than 2xing your AOV in the front end funnel.                  
```

Direct response is fundamentally a short-term game. If you can think long-term instead (AKA brand) you will crush.          Example:

```
      What if you knew that you could sell a customer a $27 low ticket product, ascend them to a $2997 program 30 days later, and then 11 MONTHS AFTER THAT they would buy your $15k/year mastermind? How much would you spend to acquire that customer?
      
      If you're thinking short term, you'd be freaking out if you spent more than $27! "Omg my ROAS!!" 
      
      But if you just ZOOMED OUT...
      
      Go ask any successful older entrepreneur "if you had a business where you could spend $3k up front, then make $15k back 12 months later, would you scale that business?"
      
      They'll look at you like you're INSANE for not doing it.
      
      (I don't need to explain the nuance here this is an illustrative example obviously focus on your cash conversion cycles but the point stands)
      
      How much do you think Athletic Greens is spending on acquiring a customer from sponsoring Joe Rogan? That fee is probably insane, but they know they're playing the LTV game                    
```

Speaking of Athletic Greens:            This is the distinction between a business opportunity and a brand. My old man finally caved on the AG1 train, he's been taking it for 2 months and is likely going to be a forever customer. At a minimum 3-4 years.

```
        You should be building brands that have staying power. That live on your customer's metaphorical kitchen counter and that becomes apart of their daily life.
        
        This is the entire concept behind the guys launching SaaS-dependant bizops. It gets a little greyhat but if your customer NEEDS your product/service to fundamentally do what they need to do, "retention" is basically automatic                      
```

Look at every multi-billion dollar company right now. Are they making their money up front by selling customers a product? Or are they making their money from data?              Alen said this – every succesful business ultimately becomes a lead gen business. Think about this a lot

```
          @RyanClogg has been talking about this a lot too. 
          
          If you build a business where another bigger business will pay you MORE for your lead than the sum total of all the products you could ever sell them... you basically have a legal money printer.
          
          Enter the world of PPC, lead gen, and big data.
          
          Oh... NOW it makes sense why all of these trillion dollar companies "sell your data" does it?                        
```

Affiliates are grossly underused at lower levels. Never seen a “growth operator” run an affiliate campaign for their creator (I’m sure they have but you get the point)                It’s a true win-win if structured correctly and ethically. Why wouldn’t you basically just promote your offer on a commission only basis?\
I wasn’t aware of the concept of “first dollar back” until recently. Game changer for bootstrapping anything                   Ex. You hire a copywriter to write a sales letter on “first dollar back” meaning you don’t pay anything up front but they get a share of the profit that comes in FIRST before you do

```
              I think this could work with a consulting model too, haven’t seen it. Ex. I’ll “waive” my $8k setup fee and get it first dollar back when we launch XYZ so it’s technically money you generated for them                            
```

Shorten your timelines                    If you had a toothache would you click on the ad that says I’ll pull your tooth in 90 seconds or 12 weeks?

```
                Also (this one comes right from Alen) you can be VERY flexible with this. Example:
                
                Option a) Start a profitable dropshipping store in 7 days or less
                
                Option b) Make $10k/mo with your dropshipping store in 6 months or less
                
                Option a could mean $100 profit but it’s still a QUICK win                              
```

SaaS rapid fire for @Finityyz
(Disclaimer: I don't have direct experience with SaaS GTM strategy; this is just my opinion as a marketer)

```
                  (Also this likely only applies to B2B not consumer apps etc.)
                  
                  If you're bootstrapped, I cannot think of any valid reason for NOT drytesting demand. It's common practice in basically every other industry. I think a lot of SaaS guys unfortunately get caught up in the ego of being a "founder" and want to invent the next Cursor. So they'd actually rather burn money on making a software that looks and sounds good that a16z would like, instead of building something customers ACTUALLY want.
                  
                  MVPs can be EXTREMELY rudimentary as long as you're up front and ethical. I know a pretty big SaaS that's a B2B lead finder for a specific vertical, and their MVP was literally just a Google Sheets. Customers aren't buying fancy UI and AI automations, they're buying a collection of verified leads they can sell to. That's what matters. So they built THAT and ran traffic to it to see if people would even want the full thing.
                  
                  Also, I know there's a difference between Software and SaaS, but I personally think every software should start as a SaaS, which should start as a service. Unless you truly have a golden opportunity and are optimizing purely for funding (which is dumb). Create a service that helps a niche, and then automate it until it's a self-sustaining software. 
                  
                  The goal should be staying power. ClickFunnels is ClickFunnels because most of the big info businesses you see out there wouldn't have been born or survived without it. They'll pay $99/mo until the end of time, or until for some reason it makes more sense to go fully self-hosted
                  
                  Becker has a LOT of truly high level game on his business channel about how he scaled Hyros. Find a group of 10 of your ideal customers, and work with them for free until your product genuinely solves their problem better than anything else on the market. Then get a cash injection by giving them a really good referral/affiliate deal and start running ads.
                  
                  Becker also says his customer support team was the biggest lever he pulled for success. Every customer had onboarding reps etc, assume they were also trying to close on year-long deals. GoHighLevel sends me fucking daily emails asking if I want to get on a free Zoom meeting with a CSM
                  
                  Also, if your goal is purely cash flow + equity, don't compete with cracked MIT grads. Go replace ancient systems in legacy industries. If I were getting into SaaS I'd be building a lead finder + nurture software for insurance agents or some shit, not fucking AI powered insert 17 year old zoomer bizop.
                  
                  Also, assuming you're smart and are focusing on finding PMF before "building" anything sophisticated, I'd probably sign on with a really good GTM agency. Fight to keep equity like your life depends on it, pay heavy up front if you had to. If I took on $300k in funding I'd give $160k of it to a cracked dev with an adderall addiction and give the rest to GTM sharks that will get my MVP out no matter what.
                  
                  Overall I think "building for equity" is a dumb idea. I know we all looked at the Figma IPO and wanted to build a shiny VC backed unicorn, but if you're ever actually going to get seroius funding / exit, it's easier to build a ruthlessly effective solution that a large customer base depends on, then pay a branding agency to package it up to look pretty for investors
```

Field Guide: From $0 to $10M - The Complete Online Education Business Roadmap
This week's Field Guide is different. Instead of focusing on one specific tactic, I'm giving you the entire playbook.

This is objectively the right path to build an 8-figure online education business from scratch. Not some theoretical framework I read in a book – this is the path I've watched dozens of offers follow to scale past $10M/year.

Fair warning: This is long.



When you finish reading this, you'll have:



A step-by-step roadmap from $0 to $10M/year with online education

The exact sequence of offers to launch (and when)

How to transition from organic to paid traffic without torching your cash

The specific metrics to track at each stage

When to hire, what to outsource, and how to not fuck it up



This isn't about launching some scrappy little offer. We're building a legitimate business here. One that scales year over year, not just spikes and dies.

Let's get into it.





Disclaimers (Because I Have To)


First: This is objectively the right path. Am I saying you're going to read this and hit $10M/year? Absolutely not. Literally zero chance. Hitting 8 figures is a 3-5 year journey, and you're going to mess up a bunch. This is just the path.

Second: This is a general overview. There's a thousand ways to do it, and you're 1,000,000% going to run into roadblocks completely different than anything here.

Third: This assumes you're either (a) an at least above-average marketer or (b) you partner with one. Solopreneurship does not exist.

Fourth: The best path is to scale what works and then pivot. If nothing's working, then maybe pivot. But every single info business ever tries a bunch of shit, it fails, one thing works (probably not what you expected), you scale the living shit out of that until it breaks, then you fix it, then you pivot.

Fifth: This is fully unbiased. I'm not trying to sell you anything, so I'm not going to tell you Facebook ads are dead because I want to sell you an organic course or vice versa.

Sixth: This doesn't cover all the infrastructure you need. You will need a sales team. You will need systems. This is what to do, not necessarily how to do every piece.

Finally: Start with being good at something. Crazy concept, I know. Selling education where you actually need to be good at the thing you're teaching.

Ideally, you're good enough that people are already asking you for help. Every great bizop VSL has that "I was doing this thing, and then all my hometown friends asked me how to get started" story. That shouldn't be an angle – it should be the truth.





Phase 1: Building Your Foundation


Step 1: Start Building Your Brand Around What You Want to Teach
Faceless offers? Don't get me started. I know they work. I've run them up myself. But we're getting to 8 figures. We're building a legitimate online education company, not some scrappy offer.

You need a brand. Even if you launch fully cold (which I've done), people will Google you. Facebook page SEO is super slept on. People are going to click on your Instagram page, Google you, check you out. Especially for higher-ticket B2B offers.



Two best ways to build your brand:



1. YouTube (The MVP)

Start TWO YouTube channels

One lifestyle/POV channel (doesn't mean flexing – means being human)

One value-focused channel (nothing held back, give everything away)

The lifestyle channel isn't about renting Lambos. It's about people getting to know YOU. If I started one, I wouldn't show my lifestyle because it's boring – I sit at my desk all day. But I'd talk about things outside of business that interest me.

People buy from humans. If they're going to send you thousands of dollars, they want to know who you are.



2. Go on Other People's Podcasts Such a hack. Especially if you're charismatic. Look at channels like Starter Story on YouTube. Those pseudo-podcast, long-form interview style channels are crushing right now.

Start building your network. Don't cold DM "yo can I get on your podcast?" Nurture relationships. Be good enough at your thing that people WANT to interview you, not just because you have followers, but because you're interesting.



Pro tip: Make a soft VSL for YouTube. Either go super highly produced (cinematic vibe, no hard sell) or raw style (Loom video, no edits, Miro board). Write a VSL without the close and without an aggressive open. Like a value webinar – pre-handle objections, walk through transformation process, bridge to solution, but keep it open-ended.



Step 2: Clip Everything


Use Opus Clip, Riverside, whatever. It's like $20/month and does it for you.

Low-key growth hack: Ask to clip the podcasts you were on. "Hey, I'd love to chop this up and share with my audience. Free growth for you." Clip it, post it, tag them, try to get reposts, add them as a contributor on Instagram. Instant authority.





Phase 2: Market Research (The Step Nobody Does)


Once you have ~1,500 followers on IG and ~700 on YouTube, it's time for the most important step that nobody does.

When you're building an offer, you don't guess. It's crazy how many people ask me "what should I sell?" I don't know. I haven't watched 100 hours of your content. Go ask your audience.



Here's exactly what to do:



Get on calls with your audience (Yes, actual calls)

Send an email or post a link asking them to get on a call

Do 10, 15, 20 calls. 30 minutes, 15 minutes, an hour – who cares?

Use a fake name/burner email if you want ("head of ops" doing market research)


Ask them real questions:

What's going on?

What are you working on?

How is that going?

What are you struggling with?

What have you tried?

Why'd you try that?

Why didn't you try this?

How can I help?


Actually help them (Don't gatekeep)

Give them real value on the call

The goal is they get so much value they don't want to hang up


Record everything and extract data:

Upload all recordings to Claude/ChatGPT

Ask it to extract the biggest shared pain points

Qualify your audience (financially, urgency of problems)

Find out what problems they have and how much they'd pay to solve them



Pro move: At the end of each call, if you've done it well enough and uncovered real pain points:

"That's awesome, dude. That's super helpful. We'll definitely take that into consideration. Transparency – I feel really good about this call because we were already building something in that direction. I've taken a lot of great stuff from this call. A lot of people are in your similar position with similar problems. I have your email – if you're interested, I'll keep you updated."

Boom. Call set. Throw them in an auto-nurture campaign.





Phase 3: Launch Your First Real Offer


Launch Round 1: One-on-One Consulting
You're a guru now. Congrats.



Key decisions:

Charge for it if you can (if your niche has money and your experience justifies it)

If you're truly starting out with no experience, do it free (but don't be that guy who charges when you shouldn't)

Cap it at 10-20 spots

Make it ACTUALLY one-on-one (not group calls disguised as 1:1)

Give them your WhatsApp, Discord channel, whatever

Time cap it (90 days is good, 30-day or 6-week sprints work too)



Why time caps matter:

You don't want people in your community 3 years later asking the same questions

Timelines create urgency (would you rather have your tooth pulled in 6 minutes or 90 days?)



During the program:

Gather generalized video testimonials (but make them LIVE demos, not scripted bullshit)

Record all your calls

Download all chat transcriptions

Track results if it's direct bizop

Do exit interviews



What you're actually doing: You're not building a course. You're solving problems. Like a personal trainer who doesn't give everyone the same workout routine – you're working with their specific problems and adjusting on the fly.





Phase 4: Create Your Scalable Program


After your first cohort, you now have two things:

A program (based on what actually worked)

Money

Take all your recordings and transcriptions. Have Claude turn them into:

Course modules/lessons

FAQ sheets

A 7-day fast start guide

Evergreen content



The problems you ended up solving probably weren't the problems they came with. Maybe you planned to help with service delivery but everyone needed help with acquisition. Maybe your entire program's success came from one cold email template you gave them.

Whatever actually worked – that's your program now.





Phase 5: Scale With A Real Funnel


Launch to Organic First
Throughout all this, you should still be:

Creating content

Uploading student testimonials

Starting your own podcast

Clipping everything



Now launch your high-ticket program:

Application VSL funnel (super standard)

Raw, super high-value VSL (not overproduced bullshit)

Typeform embedded, Calendly embedded

Take your own sales calls (at least initially)



Why take your own calls?

Way higher close rates

No disconnect between marketing and sales

You understand if your product actually helps

You hear objections directly (and can handle them in your marketing)



Then Add Low-Ticket Ascension
I'm biased toward low-ticket to high-ticket ascension. Here's why:

Benefits:

Easier to do on a low budget

Liquidates more ad spend

Buying more customers at scale

300 customers at $27 > 6 customers at $4k (for data purposes)

More people to survey, email, call, split test

Structure:

$27-97 front end

No OTOs, bumps, or bonuses initially (if you're good at marketing)

Direct to book-a-call after purchase

"One time offer: Get on the phone with me. Let's shorten this timeline."

(Shoutout to Josh Gavin for this)





Phase 6: Transition to Cold Traffic
When to Go Cold
My barometer: When I'm confident the funnel doesn't have leaks from organic.

It's not just about KPIs (though track those). It's about:

Is the funnel good?

Are the pre-call assets there?

Is the VSL good?

Are there massive bottlenecks?



How to Launch Cold
For Low-Ticket:

One campaign, one ad set, 5 ads

$50-100/day to start

Broad targeting

Dialed CAPI (Conversion API - this is crucial)

Pro tip from Alen: Add up your front end + OTOs + bumps. That total (minus high ticket) should be your daily ad budget. If ads don't suck, someone will buy your entire funnel.



For High-Ticket Book-a-Call:

Way more capital intensive

Higher risk but higher reward



Critical: Feed Facebook Quality Data
The difference between having 10 buyers Facebook knows about vs 100 buyers is the biggest leap you'll make in cold acquisition. Period.

Don't warm the pixel with people you don't want

Don't give Facebook unqualified leads

No traffic campaigns

No click campaigns

Just sales

Show Facebook who's buying and say "go find me more of those."





Phase 7: Scale Until It Breaks


This is where people fuck up. They hit $40k/month and think "time to do webinars!"

No. Just scale the living shit out of this thing.

If it's working:

10x the organic (hire agencies, clipping teams, etc.)

Scale ads aggressively (that day if metrics hold)

Don't launch new funnels

Don't change anything except volume

I've seen people at $600k/month with garbage offers just by ramming ads. If you're making $40k/month profit, add a couple zeros before you pivot.





Phase 8: Fix Your Broken Offer


When it breaks (and it will), welcome to the offer desk.

Usually it's one of two things:

Your mechanism doesn't make sense anymore

Your sales systems are too weak to handle volume



Common fixes:

Go more upmarket (remove abrasive language, sell to richer people)

Better sales reps (Oxford shirts, not 17-year-old Zoomers)

Clearer timeframes and transformations

Less educational language, more done-for-you framing

Actually listen to sales call recordings





Phase 9: Build Your Moat


At this point, you're ready to build a real business:



For the Offer:
Launch call booking to cold (you have social proof now)

Break it again and fix it again

Join 3 biggest B2C programs in your niche (competitive research)

Join 3 biggest B2B programs/masterminds (for your sales model)



For the Brand:
Build visual identity

Own digital real estate (be everywhere)

Massive content team

PR agencies, Forbes features, morning TV

Scale organic, low-ticket, and high-ticket book-a-call



Build Your Moat Around:
Your unique mechanism (that updates with current events)

Your USP

NOT your personal brand or story (those die when people stop caring)





Phase 10: The End Game


Get your AOV to $100k+

You should be able to sell something for $1 and something for $100k. If you can't, your business isn't good enough or you're in the wrong market.



Options:

Backend mastermind ($50k+/year)

Private equity plays (buy your students' businesses)

Massive affiliate plays



Build for an exit (even though info rarely exits):

Clean books

Position away from your face

Look at Athletic Greens' transformation

Scale until you're rich or dead.





The Reality Check
Most people won't make it to $10M. Not because this path doesn't work, but because:

They skip market research

They guess instead of asking their audience

They launch new offers instead of scaling what works

They hire too late (or too early)

They stop taking their own calls

They chase shiny objects



This is the path. Whether you stay on it is up to you.



– RL

Here’s Why Your Offer Isn't Selling (And How I Will Personally Fix It In 7 Days Or Less):
It has nothing to do with your copy, your website, or your traffic. 
It's a single flaw in how you built the offer in the first place – And once you see it, you'll never look at your business the same way again:
________________


Your Offer Is Wrong
You have good delivery. Solid testimonials. Tons of content.
But you can’t break past your revenue ceiling.
Maybe it’s $10k a month. Maybe it’s $100k.
Whatever it is, there is a “sticking point” that doesn’t seem to budge.
Something just feels off.
And you’re asking yourself:
“Why isn’t my offer selling?”
Truth is, it has nothing to do with your marketing, your sales skills, or your work ethic.
It’s a single, fundamental flaw in how you built your business in the first place.
And once you see it, you’ll never look at your business the same way again.
A Good Offer Is The Foundation Of Every Good Business
Your marketing, sales, website;
None of it matters unless you start from a good offer.
This isn't motivational marketing angle I’m trying to spin on you. 
This is a mechanical flaw in your machine. If the offer is broken, everything built on top of it is wasted energy.
And right now, your offer is probably broken.
Not because you're lazy. Not because you don't know marketing. Not because you haven't read enough books or taken enough courses.
Your offer is broken because you built it by looking at what other people are doing, instead of figuring out what your customer actually wants.
This document will explain why that's the problem, show you the process to fix it, and give you a way to get it fixed.
By the end of this, the decision will be obvious.
________________


So, What Actually Is An Offer? And Why Does Everyone Get It Wrong?
Most people think an offer is "what you're selling."
It's not.
An offer is what they're buying.
And people don't buy features. They buy benefits. They buy outcomes. They buy transformations.
When someone spends $60 on face cream, they're not buying face cream.
They're buying clear skin.
But they're not buying clear skin.
They're buying the confidence when they walk into a room.
But they're not buying confidence.
They're buying showing up to Thursday night drinks and making her "friends" jealous. She's buying the confidence she never had in high school because of her acne.
That's the offer.
The offer isn't "face cream." The offer is: "Click this button, enter your address, and in 30 days you will have the skin you wish you had when you were younger."
Now this skin cream isn't just skin cream. It's anti-acne skin cream. It's skin cream for people who struggled with acne their whole life.
Do you see how this shapes everything?
The ads aren't just Cover Girl-style glam shots. They're deep. They hit pain points. They bring her back to her high school years. The music, the vintage camera effects, the way people are dressed, the words they say, how the ad makes her FEEL.
See how that ALL starts from the offer?
The same goes for coaching, consulting, agency services, you name it.
You're not selling what you do. You're selling what they get. The transformation. The outcome.
Your offer needs to explain their current situation better than they even understand it themselves, and provide a solution that is SO obvious, that makes so much sense, that you don't need sleazy sales tactics or super slick copywriting.
You simply need to explain the offer to them.
This is how every great business operates.
Their "marketing" is just telling you about the offer.
Their "sales" is just someone walking you through the process, asking questions, bridging to answer those questions, and just making sure you understand the offer.
Because if the offer is so good, once they understand it, they'll sell themselves.
________________


The Problem Is Nobody Knows How To Make A Good Offer
Here's where most people go wrong.
They do "competitor research" and read Hormozi's $100M Offers book, they guarantees, bonuses, and urgency, and think they know how to make a good offer.
They did “competitor research” and saw what the gurus in their space were doing.
They hired a copywriter to make their offer “sound better.”
They ran more ads, posted more content, did more webinars.
And they're still stuck?
Why?
Because this is surface level.
They’re just consuming the articulation of the offer. They model the CORE of their business around niche angles, direct response copywriting, and good looking websites.
Not the offer.
Because here's the truth:
You don't "come up" with a good offer.
That is the biggest misconception.


Let me prove it to you.
If I asked you, right now:
"In the next 10 minutes, you need to come up with a GREAT offer that helps lawyers save money on their payroll."
What is the FIRST thing you would do?
________________


For Most People, The First Thing They Would Do Is THINK
This is wrong.
Thinking means that you assume YOU know, that YOU can "come up" with the offer.
Well, unless you are a lawyer, this is wrong.
You don't know what lawyers actually care about. You don't know what "save money on payroll" actually means to them. You don't know if that's even the real problem.
So you sit there, staring at a blank page, trying to "come up with" an offer that sounds good.
The marketer’s bias: Assuming YOU know what your audience wants.
________________


For Smarter People, They Do Competitor Research
This is better, but still wrong.
Surely somebody's already cracked this. Why reinvent the wheel?
So you Google "payroll services for law firms" and you start clicking through landing pages.
You see a bunch of different angles. Some are talking about "compliance." Some are talking about "automation." Some are talking about "time tracking."
You think, "Okay, I'll just combine the best parts of all of these."
But here's the problem:
Unless you REALLY know what to look for, you'll just get swept up in different marketing angles.
You'll be more confused than when you started.
Because you're looking at the ARTICULATION of the offer, not the offer itself.
You're looking at what they SAID, not what the customer HEARD.
________________


For Even Smarter People, They Do "Market Research"
That term gets thrown around a lot.
What does it even mean?
Are you going to read news articles? Maybe check Reddit or join a Facebook group?
You think that's ACTUALLY a good representation of their problems?
You think esteemed lawyers are just going to air out all of their problems in public?
Even if they use anonymous accounts, the average decent lawyer isn't the type to complain anyways.
You'll get a better understanding than if you just pulled it out of thin air, but you're still just going to land on surface-level answers.
You're just going to reuse their language, without understanding WHY they're saying it or WHAT they ACTUALLY MEAN by it.
"Are you spending too much money on payroll for your junior associates?"
Wow. Really cuts deep.
________________


But What Would I Do? 
I'd Go To The Source
I'd walk into a law firm.
I'd say I am interested in getting into law, and want to know what their common problems are with payroll.
Or I'd be upfront, and say I am creating a new business that helps lawyers lower their payroll costs.
I'd go right to the source. I'd call them. I'd find the bars across the street from the big firms in my city and hang out there after work hours.
I'd actually find out what their pains are.
Because once I know that, I have my offer.
I just need to create a solution to their problem, and charge for it.
It's an equal exchange.
________________


Chances Are, Your Offer Doesn't Make Sense To Your Customer
Here's what's actually happening with your business right now:
You have an offer. You've worked hard on it. You've tweaked the angles, adjusted the pricing, maybe even hired a copywriter.
You're getting some traffic. Maybe some discovery calls. Maybe even some interest.
But the conversion rate is terrible.
Something just feels off. No matter what you tweak, or how much research you do, things just don’t feel right. It feels like there’s something missing that your competitors figured out.
And you can't figure out why.
Here's why:
Your offer makes sense to YOU. It makes sense to other people in your industry. It makes sense to "business-brained" marketers who read the same books you read.
But it makes zero sense to your customer.
Because you built it by looking at what other people are doing, not by figuring out what your customer actually wants.
You're stuck in what Rene Girard calls "mimetic desire."
  

You saw what looked like a "winning offer" in your space, and you imitated it.
You created an offer that SOUNDS good to other coaches, consultants or agency owners…
…but to your ideal customer, it's just noise.
It would work on YOU, yes. But you’re not selling to you.
You’re selling to your customers.
And you’re selling them the wrong thing.
This is why you get on sales calls and hear "I can't afford it" or "I need to think about it."
This is why you launch to crickets.
This is why you feel like you're shouting into the void.
Because your offer is a copy of a copy, not an original solution to a real problem.
________________


So, What Is The Cost Of This Problem?
This isn't just an inconvenience.
This is costing you real money and real time.
Time wasted: 6-12 months (or more) spinning your wheels on an offer that was destined to fail from the start.
Money wasted: $50,000+ in ads, software, team members, courses, and other expenses trying to prop up a broken foundation.
Opportunity cost: The revenue you COULD have made if you had a good offer from the start.
Burned audience: The people who saw your offer, didn't understand it, and now won't respond to your emails or ads.
Emotional cost: The frustration, self-doubt, and fear that maybe you're just not cut out for this.
Add it all up, and a failed offer costs you $60,000 - $250,000+ in total capital and opportunity.
Your business has a fundamental capital efficiency problem. It will never scale. It is mathematically impossible.
And it's not your fault.
Nobody teaches you how to actually build an offer. They just teach you how to articulate one.
________________


The Solution: Validation, Not Imitation
So how do you fix it?
You stop guessing. You stop imitating. And you start validating.
Here's the process:
________________


Step 1: Go To The Source
If you want to know what your customer actually wants, you have to ask them.
Not in a survey. Not in a Facebook group. Not by reading Reddit threads.
You have to listen to real conversations.
If you have existing customers, you need to analyze your sales call recordings. At least 10 of them. 5 closed deals, 5 lost deals.
You need to listen to:
* How they describe their problem (in their own words)
* What they've tried before (and why it didn't work)
* What they're actually buying (the transformation, not the mechanism)
* What their objections are (and what's really behind them)
If you don't have customers yet, you need to conduct interviews. At least 10 of them. With people who fit your target niche.
You need to ask open-ended questions and LISTEN.
Don't pitch. Don't explain. Just listen.
This is the only way to build a model of what they actually want.
________________


Step 2: Identify The Real Transformation
Once you have the data, you need to figure out what they're actually buying.
This is NOT the mechanism. This is the outcome.
Use the "5 Whys" method to dimensionalize the transformation.
Example:
* "I want more leads."
* Why? "To close more deals."
* Why? "To hit my revenue target."
* Why? "To feel secure."
* Why? "To not worry about payroll."
Now you know what they're actually buying: Security. Peace of mind. Freedom from financial stress.
That's the transformation.
Not "10 leads per week." Not "a proven lead generation system."
The transformation is: "Click this button, and in 30 days you'll stop worrying about whether you can make payroll."
They are going FROM shooting into the dark, hoping one of their ad campaigns works so they don’t need to float expenses again, TO a predictable acquisition channel that they KNOW will bring in X amount of deals per month.
That's what they're buying.
________________


Step 3: Build The Offer Around The Transformation
Once you know the transformation, the rest is easy.
You just need to:
1. Articulate their current state (better than they can articulate it themselves)
2. Show them the desired state (the transformation)
3. Present the mechanism (how you'll get them there)
4. Price it relative to the value (not relative to your costs)
When you do this, something incredible happens:
Your offer stops being "a service" and becomes a solution.
Your marketing stops being "selling" and becomes educating.
Your sales calls stop being "convincing" and become enrolling.
You stop competing on price, because your offer is in a category of one.
You stop getting ghosted, because the value is obvious.
You start attracting the right clients, who are happy to pay you what you're worth.
________________


Introducing: The Offer Alignment Audit
So here's the problem:
You know your offer is broken. But you don't know HOW to fix it.
You could try to do this yourself. But if you could, you would have already.
You could hire a consultant or agency. But that's $5k-$20k+, and there's no guarantee they'll actually figure it out.
You could keep paying Facebook ad agencies or funnel experts to squeeze more revenue out of your business, but you’re just adding race fuel to a broken engine.
Or, you could pay me $497 to personally audit your offer and give you a step-by-step plan to fix it.

For just 2 hours of your time, and the price of a half-decent logo, you will fundamentally transform the single biggest contributing factor to the success of your business.
________________


By the end of this process, you will have:
1. A precise model of your niche: You will know exactly who you are serving, what they believe, and what they want.
2. A validated transformation: You will know the exact outcome they are buying, dimensionalized to the ultimate benefit.
3. An optimized price: You will know the price that maximizes revenue while remaining a no-brainer.
4. A re-engineered mechanism: You will have a mechanism that is differentiated, deliverable, and profitable.
5. A clear path to scale: You will know how to reach your niche cost-effectively.
________________


What Impact Could This Make On Your Business?
* Double your conversion rates (because the offer is now aligned with what they actually want)
* Ability to charge 50-500% more (because the transformation is clearly articulated, and they understand the true outcome they will recieve)
* Shorter sales cycles (because the offer is clear and obvious)
* Scalability (because the price and access are optimized for profitability)
________________


Think Of The ROI Of This One Change
If this audit helps you close one extra client, it pays for itself.

Why Does This Actually Work?
Because this is not a course, not coaching, and not a template.
This is a personalized, research-backed diagnosis of your specific offer, conducted by someone who understands how offers actually work.
The differentiation:

Shares the messy middle, not just the polished end result

References to god/universe/higher guidance woven naturally into practical discussions
Explores wealth as a spiritual practice, not just tactics

Thinks in systems and underlying mechanics
Questions assumptions others take as gospel
Finds depth in simple observations

Contrarian by Nature

Skeptical of mainstream business narratives
Points out what others ignore or gloss over
Not contrarian for attention—contrarian from genuine observation
Willing to say uncomfortable truths

Cadence & Structure
Sentence Flow:

Mix of short, punchy declarations and longer exploratory thoughts
Often starts with observation, builds to insight
Uses dashes and ellipses to show thinking in progress
Breaks conventional grammar rules when it serves authenticity

Opening Patterns:

"Most people don't realize..."
"Here's what nobody talks about..."
"I've been thinking about..."
"Something I noticed..."
Direct statements that set up tension

May end with question or invitation to reflect

"the thing is..."
"here's the reality..."
"most people miss this"
"nobody's talking about..."
"what actually matters"
"the real game"
"if you're paying attention"
"this is what I've learned"

References to alignment, intuition, inner knowing

Truth-seeking and authenticity
Personal sovereignty

"Let that sink in"
"Controversial but true"
"Unpopular opinion"
"Hot take"
"Here's the tea"
"Full stop"
"Period"
"This is everything"
Corporate jargon (synergy, leverage, optimize, scale—unless critiquing them)
Hustle culture language (grind, beast mode, crushing it)

"It's not X, it's Y"
Analogies and metaphors
Listicles disguised as insights
Numbered frameworks (unless genuinely useful)
Artificial cliffhangers

Business Through Spiritual Lens:

Money as energy and alignment
Building from intuition not formulas
What actually creates wealth vs. what gurus sell
The psychology of online business
Hidden mechanics of info products and creator economy

Personal Philosophy:

Enlightenment and ego dissolution
Setting boundaries with clarity
Living authentically vs. performing
Nature connection and simplicity
Questioning inherited beliefs

Market Observations:

Lesser-known opportunities in creator space
What successful people do that they don't post about
The gap between marketed success and real mechanics
Industry inefficiencies and arbitrage opportunities
Real economics behind the highlight reels

Emoji & Formatting Policy

No emojis ever
No hashtags
No thread signals (🧵, 1/, etc.)
Occasional use of:

Dashes for emphasis—like this
Ellipses for trailing thought...
Line breaks for impact
ALL CAPS sparingly for emphasis


Canadian spelling (colour, realize, centre, etc.)

What Makes It Authentic
Shows, Doesn't Tell:

Shares specific observations, not generic advice
References real experiences without fabricating credentials
Admits uncertainty and evolution of thinking
Doesn't claim to have all answers

Vulnerable Without Oversharing:

Honest about struggles and questions
Doesn't turn pain into performance
Shares lessons from failures naturally
Maintains dignity while being real

Smart Without Showing Off:

Deep thinking presented simply
Philosophical without being pretentious
Business savvy without jargon
Educated but accessible

Spiritually Integrated:

God/alignment language feels natural, not forced
Doesn't preach or convert
Treats spiritual practice as practical tool
Comfortable with mystery and not-knowing

Quality Control Questions
Before posting, ask:

Does this sound like I wrote it in my notes app at 2am?
Would I actually say this to a friend over coffee?
Am I trying to sound smart or am I genuinely exploring?
Is this insight mine or something I read and regurgitated?
Does the spiritual element feel authentic or tacked on?
Am I performing or sharing?

# Matt Gray's Guide to Viral LinkedIn Content

This document provides a comprehensive guide to creating viral content on LinkedIn, based on the frameworks and training materials developed by Matt Gray. It is designed to be a complete reference for content creators, focusing on the practical "how-to" of writing and structuring engaging posts.

## Crafting a Viral LinkedIn Post

Creating a viral LinkedIn post involves a combination of strategic content creation and audience engagement. The following sections break down the key elements of a successful post, from the initial hook to post-publication analysis.

### The Hook and Promise

The beginning of your post is critical for capturing attention. Start with a **personalized hook** that uses "I" language to make the introduction relatable. This can be further enhanced by including a specific number or statistic to grab the reader's attention. Following the hook, you must **establish a clear promise** that articulates the value the reader will gain from your post. This promise must align with the content that follows to build trust with your audience.

### Language and Readability

To ensure your content is accessible to a broad audience, **simplify your language**. The goal is to make your writing simple enough for a 5th grader to understand. This can be achieved by replacing complex words with simpler alternatives and shortening lengthy sentences. To improve readability, **organize your content into a numbered list**. This breaks down the information into a clear, digestible format. Each point in the list should directly support the main promise of your post.

### Focusing on Benefits

When writing, it is crucial to **focus on benefits over features**. Explicitly state how each feature or action benefits the reader or your audience. Use examples to illustrate the real-world impact of these benefits. This approach helps your audience understand the value of your content and how it can be applied to their own lives.

### Post-Publication Engagement

After publishing your post, it is important to **actively engage with comments** to foster discussions and maintain visibility. You should also **monitor the performance of the post** in terms of likes, reposts, and comments. By **analyzing well-performing posts**, you can identify common elements to replicate in future content.

## Effective Image Formats for LinkedIn Posts

Images can significantly increase the reach and engagement of your LinkedIn posts. This section explores three effective image formats: designed graphics, handwriting, and b-roll.

| Image Format | Description | Key Considerations |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Designed Graphics** | Polished, on-brand graphics created with design software. | Provide clear creative direction, collaborate with a designer, or create your own and have them polished. |
| **Handwriting** | Handwritten notes or drawings that add a personal touch. | Develop a daily practice, use a simple system for creation, and consider hiring a designer to systemize the process. |
| **B-Roll** | Photos and videos that align with your written topics. | Create a list of b-roll content, schedule regular shoots, and organize the content for easy access. |

## The Power of the Call-to-Action (CTA)

A strong call-to-action (CTA) is essential for encouraging reposts, driving followers, and promoting your newsletter. After your LinkedIn post has been live for 30 minutes, add a CTA that includes the following elements:

*   **Encourage Reposts:** Use a phrase like "Enjoy this? Repost it to your network" and prompt users to follow you for more content.
*   **Plug Your Newsletter:** Invite readers to join your community, mention the number of subscribers to provide social proof, and include a direct link to your newsletter sign-up page.

## Creating a Profitable LinkedIn Profile

Your LinkedIn profile is a critical component of your content strategy. A well-optimized profile can drive lead generation and revenue. The following table outlines the key elements of a profitable LinkedIn profile:

| Profile Element | Action Items |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Profile Banner** | Mention a key offering (i.e., newsletter) and include a CTA. Update the banner regularly with the latest subscriber count or promotions. |
| **Bio** | Start with your most significant achievements to build credibility. Use the Hook Stacking formula to outline the unique value you provide. Be specific and use hard numbers to demonstrate success and expertise. |
| **Strategic CTAs** | Place a primary CTA under your profile name using Creator Mode. Ensure your first bio CTA directs visitors to your newsletter. Add secondary CTAs linking to other key resources. |
| **Featured Section** | Add the two most critical links: your newsletter and your main product or service. Choose compelling, concise titles and attractive, on-brand thumbnails. |
| **Content Posting** | Develop a consistent posting schedule. Initially post without external links to avoid penalization. After 30 minutes, edit to include external links for conversion. |
| **Company Information** | Ensure your company page has a compelling description and professional logo. Encourage team members to update their profiles with the company position. |
| **Regular Updates** | Review and refresh your profile content at regular intervals. Track top-performing content and refine your strategy based on insight. |

## Generating Content Ideas

Consistently generating fresh content ideas is a common challenge. The following sections describe two powerful methods for overcoming writer's block and creating a steady stream of content.

### The 5-Year Reflection

The 5-Year Reflection is an exercise for generating content ideas by reflecting on personal experiences. By exploring seven key pillars, you can create vulnerable and resonant content that deepens your connection with your audience.

*   **Mistakes:** Share pivotal learning moments from past errors.
*   **Challenges:** Detail obstacles you have overcome and the strategies you used.
*   **Insecurities:** Be open about your fears and how you navigated them.
*   **Achievements:** Celebrate your wins to motivate others.
*   **Biggest Lessons:** Share the core principles and wisdom you have gained.
*   **Underrated Skills:** Highlight less-discussed skills that have had a significant impact.
*   **Successful Routines:** Share habits and practices that have kept you on track.

### The Content Idea Machine

The Content Idea Machine is a tool for generating a wide variety of content ideas by combining content categories with content formats. By organizing these elements in a matrix, you can quickly generate a large number of ideas.

1.  **Identify Content Categories:** Based on your target audience's needs and your unique selling proposition.
2.  **Select Content Formats:** Choose 3-4 formats to start with, such as educational, emotional, deep dives, lists, or case studies.
3.  **Create a Content Idea Matrix:** Organize your categories and formats in a spreadsheet.
4.  **Generate Ideas:** Use a ChatGPT prompt template to generate ideas for each cell in the matrix.
5.  **Refine Ideas:** Continuously refine your ideas based on audience feedback.

## The Content Waterfall System

The Content Waterfall System is a method for repurposing a single piece of long-form content into multiple pieces of content for various platforms. This system allows you to maximize your content distribution and audience reach. For example, one X thread can be turned into:

*   10 X tweets
*   3 YouTube Shorts
*   3 Instagram Reels
*   3 TikTok videos
*   3 X videos
*   1 Newsletter
*   1 Instagram Carousel
*   1 LinkedIn long-form post

## Bonus: 30 Content Templates

To help you get started, 30 days of content prompts are provided. Many of these prompts are based on high-performing content and come with a basic template that you can use to create your own version.

# WORKSHOP CONTENT OUTLINE: YOUR SECTION
## "Fix Your Offer" - The Offer Alignment Framework for Agencies

**Duration:** 45-60 minutes  
**Format:** Teaching + Live Demo Walkthroughs  
**Goal:** Show agencies how to diagnose and fix their offer misalignments using real examples

---

## OPENING HOOK (3 minutes)

### The Problem Statement

**"Why are agencies stuck at $20K/month?"**

Not because they're bad at delivery.  
Not because they need better ads.  
Not because they need more case studies.

**It's because their offer is structurally broken.**

### The Three Symptoms

1. **Commoditization** - Competing on price with every other agency
2. **Risk Reversal** - Prospects saying "too risky" or asking for pay-per-performance
3. **Timeline Mismatch** - "I'll think about it" or "Let's wait until Q2"

### The Promise

"In the next 45 minutes, I'm going to show you the exact framework I use to audit agency offers, and I'm going to walk through three real examples where I helped agencies break through their revenue ceiling by fixing one thing: their offer architecture."

---

## SECTION 1: THE OFFER ALIGNMENT FRAMEWORK (10 minutes)

### The 5 Components

Every offer has 5 components. Most agencies only think about 2 of them.

#### 1. **NICHE** - Who are you selling to?
- Not just "eCommerce" or "B2B SaaS"
- Specific ICP: revenue range, current situation, decision maker
- **Validation question:** Is there urgent demand in this niche?

#### 2. **TRANSFORMATION** - What outcome are they buying?
- Not features ("we'll run your ads")
- Not process ("we'll optimize your campaigns")
- **The emotional + logical trigger that closes the sale**
- **Validation question:** Does the market believe you can deliver this?

#### 3. **MECHANISM** - How do you deliver it?
- **Two parts most people miss:**
  - Delivery mechanism (how you fulfill)
  - Payment mechanism (how they buy)
- **Validation question:** Does the payment structure match market risk tolerance?

#### 4. **PRICE** - What does it cost?
- Not just the number
- Structure: one-time, monthly, milestone-based?
- **Validation question:** Does the price match the perceived value and risk?

#### 5. **GUARANTEE** - How do you de-risk it?
- Explicit guarantees
- Implicit de-risking (ownership, milestones, refundable deposits)
- **Validation question:** Who absorbs the risk?

### The Diagnostic Process

**For each component, mark it as:**
- ✅ **Validated** - Market evidence confirms this works
- ⚠️ **High Risk** - Market evidence shows this will suppress conversions
- ❌ **Misaligned** - Directly conflicts with market demand

**The prescription:**
- Identify the **Strongest Validation Point** (what the market desperately wants)
- Identify the **Highest Risk Assumption** (what will kill your conversions)
- Design **The Single Most Important Fix** (one high-leverage change)

---

## SECTION 2: LIVE DEMO #1 - COLLIN (GOOGLE/YOUTUBE ADS) (12 minutes)

### The Setup

**Who:** Google/YouTube Ads agency  
**Current offer:** $2.5K-$5K/month retainers  
**Revenue:** Stuck, can't scale past current client load  

### The Diagnosis

**Walk through the 5 components on screen:**

1. ✅ **Niche:** VALIDATED
   - DTC eCommerce $2M-$20M, scaled on Meta
   - Urgent demand to diversify away from Meta dependency

2. ⚠️ **Transformation:** HIGH RISK
   - Promise: "Independent new customer acquisition channel via Google"
   - **Problem:** Market doesn't believe Google = cold acquisition
   - **Evidence from sales calls:** "Google just captures warm/brand traffic"

3. ✅ **Mechanism (Delivery):** VALIDATED
   - DFY service works fine

4. ⚠️ **Mechanism (Payment) + Price/Guarantee:** HIGH RISK
   - Monthly retainer with no cold-proof de-risking
   - **Problem:** Prospect absorbs all risk, no proof it's actually cold traffic

5. **Core Objection:** "Why not just spend more on Meta?"

### The Prescription

**The Single Most Important Fix:**

Reframe from "Google Ads Management" to **"90-Day Cold Acquisition System Install"**

**Key changes:**

| Old Positioning | New Positioning |
|----------------|-----------------|
| "We'll manage your Google Ads" | "We'll install the cold acquisition system" |
| Monthly retainer | 90-day one-time install → then retainer |
| Compared to other Google agencies | Unique category: Cold Acquisition Install |
| Success = ROAS | Success = MER/nCAC (operator language) |
| Hope it works | Cold-only proof built into deliverables |

**The Deliverables (handle the objection IN the offer):**
- Brand exclusion SOPs
- Non-brand campaign structures
- nCAC/MER reporting dashboards
- Incrementality testing framework
- Attribution setup

**The Unlock:**
- Borrow all existing agency case studies (same system, different packaging)
- Price: $4K-$6K one-time (comped toward first retainer month)
- Post-BFCM launch angle: "Did Meta dependency kill your Black Friday?"

### The Result

**Before:** Competing with every Google Ads agency on price  
**After:** Own category, higher prices, handles main objection in the offer itself

---

## SECTION 3: LIVE DEMO #2 - KRISHANT (B2B OUTBOUND) (12 minutes)

### The Setup

**Who:** B2B cold email/LinkedIn outbound agency  
**Current offer:** $2,600-$7,000 upfront pilot fees  
**Problem:** Every prospect asking for pay-per-appointment, forced to negotiate down to $500/month just to close

### The Diagnosis

**Walk through the 5 components:**

1. ❌ **Niche:** MISALIGNED
   - Targeting everyone: cleaning, solar, security, consulting
   - **Problem:** Too broad = commoditized = compared to "last agency"

2. ✅ **Transformation:** ALIGNED
   - "Qualified meetings without adding headcount"
   - Market wants this

3. ❌ **Mechanism (Payment):** MISALIGNED (CRITICAL)
   - Upfront pilot fee shifts all risk to buyer
   - **Evidence from sales calls:** "Cost is not the main factor, outlaying offer is"
   - "I'm considering someone who's pay-per-appointment"
   - **The market is TELLING YOU what they want**

4. ❌ **Price/Guarantee:** MISALIGNED
   - Pricing all over the place ($7K to $500/month)
   - No risk reversal

5. **Core Objection:** "I've been burned by agencies before, I'm not paying upfront"

### The Prescription

**Two-part fix:**

**Part 1: Positioning**
"We install the **SaaS-grade outbound operating system** inside traditional B2B service firms"

**Why this works:**
- Gets OUT of comparison ("lead gen agency")
- Creates unique category (SaaS playbook transplant)
- Implies sophistication and proven results

**Part 2: Mechanism**
Replace upfront pilot with **Guardrailed Performance Pilot**

**Structure:**
- $500 refundable deposit (covers hard costs, screens unserious buyers)
- $450 per attended qualified executive meeting
- Capped at 8-12 meetings over 30 days
- Strict ICP controls (title, geo, revenue, one per account)
- No-show replacement policy
- Ascension: Convert to $4,200/month retainer or continue pay-per-appointment

**The Insight:**
"You can't stiffarm the market. They're TELLING YOU they want pay-per-performance. Give it to them, but with guardrails that protect your unit economics."

**Language shift:**
- Stop saying "pilot" (signals you're testing if it works)
- Say "Outbound OS Install" (signals you know exactly what to install)

### The Result

**Before:** Defending upfront fees, negotiating on price, losing to pay-per-appointment competitors  
**After:** Give market what they want (performance-based) with guardrails, unique positioning eliminates comparison

---

## SECTION 4: LIVE DEMO #3 - NOAH (LOCAL SEO) (12 minutes)

### The Setup

**Who:** Local SEO agency for service businesses  
**Current offer:** $2.5K-$5K/month SEO retainers  
**Problem:** Prospects saying "Are we too premature?" and "I need to see results before committing"

### The Diagnosis

**Walk through the 5 components:**

1. ✅ **Niche:** ALIGNED
   - Local service businesses $1M-$3M+ (HVAC, medspa, detailing)
   - Strong pain: inconsistent lead flow, bad agency experiences

2. ⚠️ **Transformation:** PARTIALLY ALIGNED
   - Strong emotional resonance ("dominate your local market")
   - **Problem:** Weak financial anchoring (no ROI math, no time-to-value clarity)

3. ❌ **Mechanism:** MISALIGNED (CRITICAL)
   - Retainer-first SEO with 4-6+ month ramp
   - Requires prerequisites (reviews, GBP setup, site fixes)
   - **Problem:** "Pay for months before seeing results" + "Need to fix things first" = double bind

4. ❌ **Price/Guarantee:** MISALIGNED
   - Treating prerequisites as "upsells" creates cognitive dissonance
   - Month-to-month terms clash with long SEO ramp (invites churn before payoff)

5. **Core Objection:** "I'll never sign a contract again" + "Are we too premature to start?"

### The Prescription

**The Single Most Important Fix:**

Replace retainer-first with **"Local Dominance Sprint"** (10-12 weeks, DFY one-time)

**The Deliverables:**
- GBP creation/ownership transfer
- Full GBP optimization
- Review engine setup (templates, automation)
- Site/on-page fixes for top money pages
- Citations/NAP cleanup
- Baseline and 45-day heatmaps
- Tracking/attribution setup
- Transition/offboarding support from prior agency

**Pricing:**
- $3.5K-$5K (single location) or $5K-$8K (multi-location)
- Milestone billing: 60% kickoff / 40% completion
- **Guarantee:** "If we don't deliver documented Sprint deliverables within 12 weeks, final 40% is waived"

**Ascension Paths:**
- **Track A:** Google Ads Management (fast lead flow, 30-day ROI)
- **Track B:** SEO Authority-Build (compounding demand, 6-12 month path)

**The Insight:**
"80% of the work you do in a 6-month retainer happens in month 1 anyway. You're already doing the Sprint, you're just packaging it wrong and spreading the billing across six months, which makes the math not work for the buyer."

**The Reframe:**
"Pay once to own the engine, then pay monthly if you want us to drive it"

### The Result

**Before:** Timing objections, prerequisite blockers, contract aversion  
**After:** Finite commitment, quick wins, client owns assets, clear ascension path

---

## SECTION 5: THE UNIVERSAL PATTERNS (8 minutes)

### Pattern 1: The Retainer → Install → Retainer Model

**The problem with retainer-first:**
- Prospect absorbs all risk
- Long time to results
- Compared to other agencies
- "Hope it works" mentality

**The solution:**
- Productized installation (finite, deliverable-based)
- Client owns the assets
- Quick wins and baselines
- THEN ascend to retainer (after trust is earned)

**The math:**
Most agency work happens in first 60 days (setup, systems, baselines). Package that as a one-time install, then ongoing management becomes an easy upsell.

### Pattern 2: Language is EVERYTHING

**Bad language (increases perceived effort):**
- "Mentorship," "coaching," "we'll teach you"
- "Build your system"
- "Step-by-step guidance"
- "Pilot" (signals testing)

**Good language (decreases perceived effort):**
- "Install," "plug-and-play," "steal our system"
- "Done-for-you," "access to"
- "Operating System Install"

**The difference:**
"I'll show you how to change your oil" vs. "I'll change your oil for you"

Same backend work. Radically different perceived value.

### Pattern 3: Handle Objections IN the Offer

**Don't try to overcome objections with better sales skills.**

**Build the solution to the objection into the deliverables.**

**Examples:**
- Collin: "Google = warm traffic" → Cold-only proof mechanisms in deliverables
- Krishant: "Too risky upfront" → Refundable deposit + pay-per-meeting
- Noah: "Too premature" → Prerequisites bundled into Sprint

### Pattern 4: Stop Competing, Start Creating

**If you position as:**
- "Google Ads agency"
- "Lead gen agency"
- "SEO agency"

**You're compared to every other agency in that category.**

**Result:** Compete on price and terms.

**Solution:** Create a unique category through mechanism + positioning.

**Examples:**
- "Cold Acquisition System Install with MER/nCAC Proof"
- "SaaS-Grade Outbound OS Transplant"
- "Local Dominance Sprint"

### Pattern 5: The Market is Always Right

**When prospects repeatedly say:**
- "Can you do pay-per-performance?"
- "This feels too risky"
- "Are we too premature?"

**They're not giving objections.**

**They're telling you the offer is wrong.**

You can't overcome this with better copy or closing skills. You need a different offer structure.

---

## SECTION 6: YOUR ACTION PLAN (5 minutes)

### Step 1: Audit Your Current Offer

Run it through the 5 components:

- **Interactive on action plan** (get them thinking about their own offer)

### Energy

- **Confident, not salesy** (you're diagnosing, not pitching)
- **Evidence-based** (constantly reference the sales calls and market feedback)
- **Generous** (give away the methodology, hold back the implementation)

### Transitions

- **Between demos:** "See the pattern? Let's look at a completely different niche..."
- **To action plan:** "Now it's your turn. Here's exactly how to do this for your own offer..."
- **To close:** "This is the methodology. These are real examples. This works."

---

## ALIGNMENT WITH WORKSHOP PHILOSOPHY

### Anti-Guru Positioning
- ✅ Real client examples (not made-up case studies)
- ✅ Show the actual work (audit reports, call transcripts)
- ✅ Prove competence through methodology (not Miami balconies)

### Diagnostic Approach
- ✅ Help them self-diagnose their misalignment
- ✅ Exit survey routes them to appropriate solution
- ✅ Clarity over transformation (at $97 price point)

### Generous Education
- ✅ Give away the framework
- ✅ Show the live examples
- ✅ Provide actionable templates
- ✅ Still converts (Ryan Clog model)

### Collaborative Nature
- ✅ Complements Clint's sales/infrastructure content
- ✅ Sets up ascension to your offer, Michael's SaaS offer, Clint's offer
- ✅ Cross-referencing throughout ("Clint will show you the math on this...")

---

## POST-WORKSHOP ASCENSION

### Exit Survey Questions

1. "What's your current monthly revenue?"
2. "What's your current offer structure?" (retainer/one-time/hybrid)
3. "What's your biggest bottleneck right now?"
   - [ ] My offer is commoditized (competing on price)
   - [ ] My close rate is too low (risk/objections)
   - [ ] My delivery is too manual (can't scale)
   - [ ] I need to add a new revenue stream

4. "Based on what you learned, what's your next step?"
   - [ ] Fix my current offer positioning
   - [ ] Add a productized installation offer
   - [ ] Launch a new offer to a different segment
   - [ ] Get a full offer audit

### Routing Logic

**If "commoditized" + "fix positioning"** → Your offer audit service  
**If "need new revenue stream" + "SaaS"** → Michael's offer  
**If "delivery too manual" + "infrastructure"** → Clint's offer  
**If "close rate too low"** → Combination (your audit + Clint's sales)

---

## FINAL NOTES

This content is **live demo heavy**, which aligns perfectly with the workshop philosophy of "show, don't tell." You're not teaching theory - you're walking through real transformations with real clients.

The three examples cover different niches (eCommerce, B2B, local services) and different problems (transformation skepticism, risk allocation, timeline mismatch), which shows the framework is universal.

The action plan is concrete and immediately actionable (72-hour validation test), which gives them a clear next step even if they don't buy anything.

This positions you as the "offer guy" in the trio, complements Clint's "infrastructure/math guy" positioning, and sets up natural cross-referrals.

# Claude Prompt: Personal Brand Twitter Content Generation

**You are an expert ghostwriter for a personal brand on Twitter (X).** Your task is to generate Twitter content (long-form threads and short-form tweets) that embodies a raw, unfiltered, authentic, and conversational tone, while being strategically structured to drive engagement and leads for the user's `webuildyouroffer` group and upcoming paid offers. **Crucially, you must avoid any language or structure that sounds AI-generated or overly theatrical, and instead capture the user's unique, human voice.**

## User's Brand Context & Goal:

The user is a ghostwriter at a top Twitter growth agency, with a personal brand centered around online marketing, infoproducts, general business, and lifestyle. They have recently experienced meteoric growth by positioning themselves as a guru more, but want to avoid becoming 100% 'guru mode'. The goal is to increase output to one long-form post and three shorter tweets daily, supplemented by organic, off-the-cuff content. The content should drive engagement, grow the audience, and convert followers into leads for the `webuildyouroffer` group, the upcoming $497 consulting offer, and future high-ticket information products.

## Core Principles:

This strategy blends the user's raw authenticity and philosophical depth with a structured, lead-generating approach. The aim is to leverage the strength of recent growth (from more structured posts about business and knowledge) while avoiding the 'guru mode' that feels inauthentic.

## Key Learnings from User's Original Tweets (Analysis Summary):

*   **Engagement Drivers**: Highest-performing tweets often involve direct engagement, strong opinions, and sometimes a touch of controversy or personal revelation. Content related to "online marketing" and "personal growth" performs well, but direct promotion of `webuildyouroffer` also shows high engagement when done effectively.
*   **Tonality**: Neutral and slightly negative sentiment tweets tend to have higher average likes, indicating that a raw, critical, or challenging tone resonates. Positive tonality is less effective.
*   **Tweet Length**: Slightly longer, more developed thoughts tend to perform better. High-engagement tweets have an average word count of ~31 words and average sentence length of ~23 words.
*   **Writing Style**: Frequent use of contractions (~55%) contributes to a conversational tone. Questions (~15%) are effective engagement drivers. The user successfully avoids the "It's not X, it's Y" pattern.
*   **Recent Growth**: The last 3 months show significantly higher average likes and views, confirming the effectiveness of the user's shift towards more structured business/knowledge posts.

## Key Learnings from User's Personal Claude Instructions:

*   **Voice**: Raw, unfiltered, personal revelations, counterintuitive truths, real-time insights, Canadian English, avoiding corporate/polished language, **no emojis/hashtags**.
*   **Content**: Blend personal growth with business, philosophy, nature, authentic living, lesser-known business aspects, real struggles, personal evolution, psychological aspects of building wealth, subtle spirituality/alignment.
*   **Avoid**: "It's not X, it's Y" format, analogies, manufactured engagement hooks, generic business advice, excessive optimization, forced motivation, thread signals (🧵).
*   **Authentic Elements**: Skepticism of mainstream narratives, enlightenment, personal boundaries, lifestyle design, natural health practices, critique of superficial business trends, raw honesty.

## Key Learnings from Client Project Instructions (Shaun Ghavami):

*   **Objective**: Craft viral-grade threads matching client's voice, driving growth, engagement, conversions, and establishing industry leadership.
*   **Core Elements**: Include industry specifics, reference validated numbers (only if verifiable), conversational/authentic tone, clear value proposition.
*   **Storytelling**: Personal journey, industry insight/analysis, operational philosophy.
*   **Technical Formatting**: Threads MAX 10 tweets (aim 6-8), tweets under 280 characters, specific bullet points (•) for lists (no indents), full stop separation between tweets for Notion pasting.
*   **Voice & Language**: Conversational, like talking to a friend, avoid unnatural structures (e.g., "it's not X, it's Y", "the reason? it's X"), casual but credible, pithy and persuasive without being pushy, use contractions.
*   **Content Requirements**: Actionable insight, mix business with personal views, real/verifiable numbers, structured for online consumption, tangible value.
*   **Hook Guidelines**: 2-4 short, punchy lines; attention-grabbing start; promise/transition; include revenue numbers, timeframes, personal story, contrasts, bold statements, universal truths.
*   **Anti-AI Guidelines**: Avoid anything that sounds AI-generated (e.g., specific sentence structures, overuse of em dashes, theatrical language).

## Analysis of Unsatisfactory Claude Output (Provided by User):

The previous Claude output failed to capture the authentic voice due to:

*   **Overly Theatrical and Manufactured Tone**: Language felt forced and overly dramatic, e.g., "Most info guys are terrified..." This contradicts the user's preference for raw, unfiltered, and conversational.
*   **Repetitive and Formulaic Structure**: Predictable patterns in thread hooks and transitions made content feel templated, not genuine personal insights.
*   **Lack of Nuance and Depth**: Content lacked philosophical depth, skepticism, and raw honesty. It leaned into generic business advice.
*   **Absence of Specificity and Personal Anecdotes**: Lacked the specific, compelling real-world examples found in the user's own tweets.
*   **Generic Calls to Action**: CTAs were generic and lacked subtle integration.
*   **Incorrect Formatting**: Used bullet points within threads in a way that didn't align with the client guidelines for lists.

**Your Role**: You are an expert ghostwriter for a personal brand on Twitter (X). Your primary directive is to generate content that sounds indistinguishable from the user's own writing, blending their raw, authentic voice with a structured, lead-driving approach. 4.  **Philosophical Undercurrent**: Blend personal growth insights with business applications. Draw from philosophy, nature connection, and authentic living. A subtle tinge of spirituality/alignment with a higher purpose can be sprinkled in.

2.  **General Business & Entrepreneurship**: Realities of building wealth online, entrepreneurship, offer optimization, and the business landscape. Insights from partnering with coaches, consultants, and community owners.
