Apparently everyone misses the "OG Money Twitter" days so I'm starting a thread of pure high-level online marketing tips that I'll be adding to throughout the day.

Enjoy:  When you're trying to drive real ROI with organic traffic (especially video-focused platforms like YouTube and TikTok), you need to put yourself in the shoes of the platform.

  With something like paid Facebook ads, the "win-win" is pretty clear: You pay them for their advertising space, and in return they show your content to your potential customers. They spend billions of $ a year aggregating data, so you can have the absolute best results possible. It is called an "auction" for a reason – the more you spend, the more they'll distribute your content.  But what about organic platforms that you don't pay for? What are you going to give these platforms in return for showing customers your content?  Well, think to the example above – these platforms get paid through advertisments. The more advertising revenue they can make, the better.   So, if you're not going to pay them directly, you need to help them generate as much revenue as possible from people who ARE paying them.  This is where the idea of "retention" comes in. If your organic content makes viewers stay on the platform 2x as long, that's 2x more advertising space they can sell, which means it's in the PLATFORMS' best interest to show your content to more people.   This is why the meta on YouTube right now is linking other videos on your channel in your video description.  Think back to when everyone started only posting 10+ minute videos. Some people were adding blank space to the end just to get it over the 10min mark. There was a direct ROI in ad revenue.   YouTube is the strongest example of this but it goes for other platforms. This is why TikTok creators will do "Part 1" of a video, cut it off, then post Part 2, Part 3 etc.   Remember you're not just "posting content' you're directly contributing to an advertising/data monopoly. You need to pay the piper    Market awareness is way up in bizop. CPCs are 2-3x higher than they were a few years ago. Everyone is competing for the same limited space with the same angles. You can't "trick" the market anymore. Nobody is getting on a webinar without EXPECTING there to be a pitch. If you run whitehat live webinars, you'll see comments flooding with "where's the pitch course scammer!" If you're selling high awareness B2B, just drop the gimmicks altogether. Go extremely mechanistic, explain why YOUR solution is better, newer, safer, easier than your competitors. Explain what is currently happening in the world, politics, economy, technology, social trends etc. that enables your solution. Study old Agora angles, it was usually "This [thing happening in the world] is letting people like you achieve [outcome]" If you're selling a high ticket sales program, it's unlikely you're getting a flood of people who have NEVER heard of HTS before. So you have two options: a) Create a new angle altogether and go low awareness. Drop the HTS. There was a program (forget which one) that framed it as becoming a "digital customer service representative" where you helped potential customers understand the program, get the support they need, collect payments and onboard them into the community
 b) Create a new unique mechanism that beats everything else. Why is yours fundamentally different than the competition? Why did the programs they already purchase not work for them?      
Market awareness part 2.    If selling B2C or 0-1 bizop, again just assume most of your buyers have gone through some sort of make money online funnel and don't try to trick them.    The main focus here is congruency and HONESTY.   The reason everyone's moving away from opt ins on BAC funnels is the same reason as the last tweet – they know you're not giving them a "free training" that "reveals" their secret. You're just collecting their email, sending them to a VSL and hammering them with emails.   Even if they don't know this directly from experience, they have suspision you're selling them something.   If you want them to book a call, let them book a call. Just put the calendar right underneath the VSL. Or have a button that just says "Click Here To Apply ->" that takes them right to the app.        
The best "retargetting" you can do is just being the person they want to buy from. This means having a brand. Whether that's with a big organic following, or a shit ton of retargetting ads When you're doing a typical opt-in -> book a call -> email follow ups to get them to book, all you're REALLY doing is getting the people who were 70% of the way to booking but didn't over the edge.
 
 If someone was NOT interested in booking (or purchasing) because you fundamentally didn't get them to trust you, or explain why your solution was right for them well enough, a 5 day email sequence is NOT going to suddenly shift their entire belief structure.
 
 Sales cycles are long. It's a barbell theory – either people are already mentally bought in and need follow ups to just take the action, or they're NOT bought in and require a LOT more time spent with you (content)
 
 Do you think people are buying from Brez because he has an extremely dialled follow-up sequence, or because he's fucking EVERYWHERE and is top of mind 24/7 for his target audience?          
Follow up to the above: you can run retargetting ads using your best performing organic content for DIRT cheap. Facebook knows who to show it to (obviously) and they likely just need to trust you more, so don't just hammer them with sales copy but actually NURTURE them            
Maybe the most important one:     ACTUALLY put yourself into your buyers' shoes. Most never do this. They just run copy angles that they "know works" and never ACTUALLY remove their personal bias.
     
     Think of the last time YOU made a 5-figure investment. Was it REALLY because of a razor sharp direct response campaign? Or did you just SEE the person for months, consume a lot of their content, hear other people say "yeah he's the best" etc.
     
     What % of Jeremy Haynes' mastermind customers bought DIRECTLY because of an ad campaign? How many of them were TRUE cold prospects? I'd best majority are in there because it's just KNOWN that that's where you go to get the best info. It is a ripple effect of social proof that nurtures you even when you're not directly consuming activation material              
Spaces that were saturated 3-4 years ago are basically blue oceans again when everyone jumped ship to make money online/SaaS/AI etc.       Iman was teaching Facebook ads for local businesses and it got giga saturated. Now everyone's just trying to be a growth operator for growth operators. 
       
       If you can actually drive traffic, you can pitch law firms and doctors offices on 5x the retainers you can for a 17 year old selling ecom automation                
90% of the BIGGEST levers you can pull to increase ROAS on your ads are NOT in the ads manager.         There are baseline benchmark metrics everybody's basically hitting. If you are running good ads to a good offer, it's unlikely your ad metrics are going to be SIGNIFICANTLY different from competitors of your size. Lots of nuance here obviously but the point stands
         
         So, the absolute BIGGEST lever you can pull is LTV, and 7 day cash collected. This was basically the entire point of Hormozi's latest launch.
         
         Again, assuming you're running a decently optimized campaign, slashing your CPA in 1/2 by tweaking your ads is SIGNIFICANTLY more difficult than 2xing your AOV in the front end funnel.                  
Direct response is fundamentally a short-term game. If you can think long-term instead (AKA brand) you will crush.          Example:
          
          What if you knew that you could sell a customer a $27 low ticket product, ascend them to a $2997 program 30 days later, and then 11 MONTHS AFTER THAT they would buy your $15k/year mastermind? How much would you spend to acquire that customer?
          
          If you're thinking short term, you'd be freaking out if you spent more than $27! "Omg my ROAS!!" 
          
          But if you just ZOOMED OUT...
          
          Go ask any successful older entrepreneur "if you had a business where you could spend $3k up front, then make $15k back 12 months later, would you scale that business?"
          
          They'll look at you like you're INSANE for not doing it.
          
          (I don't need to explain the nuance here this is an illustrative example obviously focus on your cash conversion cycles but the point stands)
          
          How much do you think Athletic Greens is spending on acquiring a customer from sponsoring Joe Rogan? That fee is probably insane, but they know they're playing the LTV game                    
Speaking of Athletic Greens:            This is the distinction between a business opportunity and a brand. My old man finally caved on the AG1 train, he's been taking it for 2 months and is likely going to be a forever customer. At a minimum 3-4 years.
            
            You should be building brands that have staying power. That live on your customer's metaphorical kitchen counter and that becomes apart of their daily life.
            
            This is the entire concept behind the guys launching SaaS-dependant bizops. It gets a little greyhat but if your customer NEEDS your product/service to fundamentally do what they need to do, "retention" is basically automatic                      
Look at every multi-billion dollar company right now. Are they making their money up front by selling customers a product? Or are they making their money from data?              Alen said this – every succesful business ultimately becomes a lead gen business. Think about this a lot
              
              @RyanClogg has been talking about this a lot too. 
              
              If you build a business where another bigger business will pay you MORE for your lead than the sum total of all the products you could ever sell them... you basically have a legal money printer.
              
              Enter the world of PPC, lead gen, and big data.
              
              Oh... NOW it makes sense why all of these trillion dollar companies "sell your data" does it?                        
Affiliates are grossly underused at lower levels. Never seen a “growth operator” run an affiliate campaign for their creator (I’m sure they have but you get the point)                It’s a true win-win if structured correctly and ethically. Why wouldn’t you basically just promote your offer on a commission only basis?                          
I wasn’t aware of the concept of “first dollar back” until recently. Game changer for bootstrapping anything                   Ex. You hire a copywriter to write a sales letter on “first dollar back” meaning you don’t pay anything up front but they get a share of the profit that comes in FIRST before you do
                  
                  I think this could work with a consulting model too, haven’t seen it. Ex. I’ll “waive” my $8k setup fee and get it first dollar back when we launch XYZ so it’s technically money you generated for them                            
Shorten your timelines                    If you had a toothache would you click on the ad that says I’ll pull your tooth in 90 seconds or 12 weeks?
                    
                    Also (this one comes right from Alen) you can be VERY flexible with this. Example:
                    
                    Option a) Start a profitable dropshipping store in 7 days or less
                    
                    Option b) Make $10k/mo with your dropshipping store in 6 months or less
                    
                    Option a could mean $100 profit but it’s still a QUICK win                              
SaaS rapid fire for @Finityyz
                       (Disclaimer: I don't have direct experience with SaaS GTM strategy; this is just my opinion as a marketer)
                      
                      (Also this likely only applies to B2B not consumer apps etc.)
                      
                      If you're bootstrapped, I cannot think of any valid reason for NOT drytesting demand. It's common practice in basically every other industry. I think a lot of SaaS guys unfortunately get caught up in the ego of being a "founder" and want to invent the next Cursor. So they'd actually rather burn money on making a software that looks and sounds good that a16z would like, instead of building something customers ACTUALLY want.
                      
                      MVPs can be EXTREMELY rudimentary as long as you're up front and ethical. I know a pretty big SaaS that's a B2B lead finder for a specific vertical, and their MVP was literally just a Google Sheets. Customers aren't buying fancy UI and AI automations, they're buying a collection of verified leads they can sell to. That's what matters. So they built THAT and ran traffic to it to see if people would even want the full thing.
                      
                      Also, I know there's a difference between Software and SaaS, but I personally think every software should start as a SaaS, which should start as a service. Unless you truly have a golden opportunity and are optimizing purely for funding (which is dumb). Create a service that helps a niche, and then automate it until it's a self-sustaining software. 
                      
                      The goal should be staying power. ClickFunnels is ClickFunnels because most of the big info businesses you see out there wouldn't have been born or survived without it. They'll pay $99/mo until the end of time, or until for some reason it makes more sense to go fully self-hosted
                      
                      Becker has a LOT of truly high level game on his business channel about how he scaled Hyros. Find a group of 10 of your ideal customers, and work with them for free until your product genuinely solves their problem better than anything else on the market. Then get a cash injection by giving them a really good referral/affiliate deal and start running ads.
                      
                      Becker also says his customer support team was the biggest lever he pulled for success. Every customer had onboarding reps etc, assume they were also trying to close on year-long deals. GoHighLevel sends me fucking daily emails asking if I want to get on a free Zoom meeting with a CSM
                      
                      Also, if your goal is purely cash flow + equity, don't compete with cracked MIT grads. Go replace ancient systems in legacy industries. If I were getting into SaaS I'd be building a lead finder + nurture software for insurance agents or some shit, not fucking AI powered insert 17 year old zoomer bizop.
                      
                      Also, assuming you're smart and are focusing on finding PMF before "building" anything sophisticated, I'd probably sign on with a really good GTM agency. Fight to keep equity like your life depends on it, pay heavy up front if you had to. If I took on $300k in funding I'd give $160k of it to a cracked dev with an adderall addiction and give the rest to GTM sharks that will get my MVP out no matter what.
                      
                      Overall I think "building for equity" is a dumb idea. I know we all looked at the Figma IPO and wanted to build a shiny VC backed unicorn, but if you're ever actually going to get seroius funding / exit, it's easier to build a ruthlessly effective solution that a large customer base depends on, then pay a branding agency to package it up to look pretty for investors

data.content:
Field Guide 02: The 10 Minute Offer Fix Exercise
Intro

When I had to think of a witty tagline for WBYO, I came up with:

“What you sell is fine. How you sell it isn’t.”

I’ve heard better. But it’ll stick.

The idea behind it is summarizing my entire philosophy on offers.

The only thing that matters about the product is that it gets damn good results for your customers. It has nothing to do with how well the offer sells.

How you sell it (AKA the positioning, the framing, the messaging, does)

Example:

Which product sounds better:

We teach you how to make $10k/mo in High Ticket Sales in 90 days

XYZ is a sales rep placement agency. We partner with consulting firms doing $500k/year+ to assign and train elite sales reps into their businesses. We genuinely cannot keep up with the demand, and have more deals in our pipeline than we do sales reps able to take on $10k/mo+ positions. Given our extensive training protocols, we take complete beginners, transform them into elite sales reps, and place them on a deal in our pipeline in 90 days or less

Yes, option B is longer. But it also makes more sense. It’s clearer to understand. The “okay, but what’s in it for you? Where’s the catch?” is answered.

If your offer requires 3 paragraphs, a Miro board, and explaining “it’s complicated,” the market will punish you.

This week’s Field Guide gives you a 10 minute exercise I run with businesses that cleans all that up, and unlocks conversions fast.

We’re going to make your offer kindergarten-simple, without dumbing it down.

When you finish, you’ll have:

A one-line offer anyone can understand

A 3 sentence “what/why/how” explainer you can paste on your landing page, or add to your VSL

A plain English mechanism line that makes your offer feel inevitable

New hero copy, ad hooks, and VSL/TSL leads that convert better (because they’re crysta clear”

If you do this, you will immediately see lifts in clicks, time on page, booking rates, and close rates

Why this works

People buy what they understand. Confused visitors don’t convert

Clarity raises perceived value. When the path is obvious the price resistance drops

Simple travels farther. Affiliates, partners, and customers can repeat a simple offer. This is how offers go “viral” – if people can repeat it to their friends at lunch, then it can spread through word of mouth (we will talk about Kozmin’s idea of the Viral Sales Letter in a later Field Guide)

The Feynman principle: if you can’t explain it simply, you don’t really understand it. Richard Feynman’s entire teaching philosophy was clarity-as-proof-of-understanding. This exercise applies that to your business

The 10-Minute Test:

(Actually do this. I never do these “exercises” when I see them either, but trust me. Don’t do it in your head or do it later. Just do it after you read it)

Set a timer for 10 minutes.

Open a blank doc.

DON’T use jargon, acronyms, or “it depends.”

1. Write your current offer in 1 sentence (60 seconds)

Use this as a starting point:

“We help \[who] get \[result] in \[timeframe], without \[dreaded thing]”

Side note: This is how most people’s offers FINISH. I see this headline, cold email script, etc. literally everywhere. I’m pretty sure Hormozi popularized it in his $100M Offers book. It works, but it’s the STARTING POINT

If that takes you more than a minute, your offer is already too complicated.

1. Do the dinner table test (3 minutes)

Imagine you’re at your good friend’s house. Mom asks, “So what actually IS your business?”

Answer in three sentences, max:

What is it? One simple sentence

How does it work? Two steps, max

Why is it good? Plain, tangible upside

Rules:

No jargon. If a 13-year-old wouldn’t know the word, swap it

No humble brag “oh it’s complicated.” If you can’t explain it, the offer isn’t ready

No outcomes without mechanism. “We get you clients” is incomplete. Tell me “how”

Template:

What: “I run a \[type of thing] that helps \[who] \[do what specific thing]”

How: “We do it by \[plain-English mechanism in 1–2 steps]”

Why: “It’s good because \[short, concrete benefit: faster, cheaper, easier, safer, more certain]”

Strip to first principles (2 minutes)

If you don’t know the definition of first principles thinking, Google it. I’ll dive into it in another Field Guide

Now remove every word you wouldn’t use with a child:

Replace “acquisition” with “get customers”

Replace “conversion optimization” with “make more visitors buy”

Replace “pipeline” with “list of people we follow up with”

Replace “n8n workflows” with “automated action”

Replace “SaaS” with “software”

Replace “LTV/ARPU/CAC” with “how much each customer pays us,” “average per customer,” “what it costs to get a customer”

Note: Yes, I know, that’s too simple. if you’re in a high awareness, sophisticated market, maybe M\&A or legal, you will want to use the appropriate language. That isn’t the point of this exercise. We’ll do a separate Field Guide on market adjacent tonality. The goal of this is for YOU to understand your offer so well, and be able to explain it to the average person. Not to write your ad copy

1. Mechanism in a sentence (1 minute)

Write the mechanism like you’d explain dropshipping to your parents:

“When someone buys, we take their order and send it directly to the supplier, who ships it to the customer. We keep the difference.”

Package the outputs (1 minute) You should now have:

One-line offer

3-sentence what/how/why

Mechanism sentence

This can now serve as your foundation for everything you write. Whether ads, VSLs, headlines, etc.

A lot of people get into their particular business in weird, obscure ways. Maybe someone reaches out and asks to partner, maybe they fall into it, maybe they see an ad for a course and decide to try it out.

Whatever it is – people rarely start by sitting down, objectively looking at everything, and carefully constructing a good offer.

Most of the time, the plane is built on the way up.

With this, they get so used to running and gunning, solving problems as they pop up, that they don’t take 10 minutes to sit down, strip everything back, and realign with the CORE of their business.

Practical Applications:

Headlines:

I built an offer that was basically a funnel and CRM template for creators. I was initially running the more DWY angle, like “we’ll show you how to get sales from your Instagram.” But when I did this exercise, I realized the offer was actually DFY. “We’ll SHOW YOU” implies learning, it implies they need to WATCH, which makes perceived effort higher, which makes conversions drop (it was a low ticket offer).

As I did the exercise, it was actually a “Plug and Play” solution.

So, the headline became:

“2,317 Creators Used This $20 Plug‑n‑Profit Funnel to Make Their First Sale Online – Copy, Paste, and Launch a Self-Selling Sales Machine in 15 Minutes.”

“✓‎ ‎ Self-Selling Sales Machine ‎ ✓ ‎ 1‑Click Setup ‎ ✓ ‎ Templates Included ‎ ✓ ‎ Live in 15 Minutes”

Without the exercise, I would’ve never uncovered that fully DFY “Plug and Play” framing, which when running a mass market bizop offer (we wanted big TAM for the “creators” on IG), crushes.

Ads:

For ads, there are a few ways you can use this.

The most basic and obvious is just running straight mechanistic ad copy.

Example:

“If you’re a creator, you could have a fully plug and play system setup to sell your digital products or coaching in the next 15 minutes”

Or “We will give you a fully plug and play website and selling system to XYZ”

Or whatever we decide to run.

Another great way is, once you have your mechanism dialled, just plugging it in into existing frames or angles.

Example:

I saw a statistic last week that the average digital creator makes less than minimum wage (ridiculously fire cold traffic angle). So, now that the mechanism is dialled, its super easy to just antagonize and then bridge to solution. Call out painpoint (basically just say the statistic) then let them know they can fix it in the next 15 minutes

Emails:

I’ll have to do a whole separate Field Guide on emails because most people get them wrong.

But for campaigns, they almost function similar to ads (in my opinion) – I’m usually just trying to find new ways to reiterate the mechanism, or finding unique angles, news stories, current events, fun ideas etc. to open curiosity and agitate pain points, and then since the mechanism is dialled, super easy to CTA back to the VSL to learn more.

I’d probably rip an email to this list with the subject line “The 3-sentence offer that sells itself:” for this Field Guide. Notice how that’s just an extraction of the mechanism.

Bonus Tip: FAQ Section on Funnel

FAQs are so slept on. I’ve been experimenting with adding 20+ FAQs to the bottom of my funnels, both warm and cold. They should essentially function as pre-objection handlers (the most common objections raised on sales calls).

Understanding your offer fundamentally allows you to have super dialled FAQs.

Examples:

“What exactly is this?” Answer in one sentence.

“How does it work?” Two steps, no jargon.

“Why is it better?” One clear, specific advantage.

“How long until I see results?” Honest timeframe.

“What if it doesn’t work?” Your risk reversal.

Note: Actual FAQs should be more specific than this

Before/After examples across niches:

Coaches/Consultants

Before: “We’re an elite growth consultancy installing bespoke GTM systems to 10x your MRR.”

After: “We help B2B coaches get 5–10 sales calls a week by turning their best content into one simple offer and running ads to it. We set up the funnel and follow-ups so calls keep coming in without you posting more.”

Community Owners

Before: “We run a transformative Skool community with live calls, frameworks, and accountability.”

After: “We help your members hit one specific win in 30 days with a guided sprint. They get a checklist, a weekly call, and we track progress. You keep your community fees and make 3–5x more per member.”

Agency

Before: “Full-stack demand gen across omni-channel paid and lifecycle.”

After: “We write one page that explains your offer clearly and run ads to it. We follow up with everyone who clicks until they book a call. You get more calls from the same ad budget.”

SaaS

Before: “We offer end-to-end data-driven workflow automation with AI agents and LLM orchestration.”

After: “Our software watches your inbox, fills your CRM, and sends the next email for you. Your team spends time closing, not copying and pasting.”

Ecom

Before: “Premium performance nutraceuticals leveraging mitochondrial optimization and circadian science.”

After: “We sell a drink mix that stops afternoon crashes. Stir into water at 2 pm. Tastes great and helps you focus for 3–4 hours without jitters.”

Newsletter/Media

Before: “A multifaceted content business monetized through omni-channel brand partnerships.”

After: “We write one great email each week and sell the middle spot to a brand your readers already buy. They pay us, you get useful recommendations, and we stay free.”

Common mistakes and how to fix them

Mistake: Listing features, not the job.

Fix: State the one job customers hire you to do in their words.

Mistake: Vanity complexity.

Fix: Force the two-step mechanism. If you need step 3–5 to explain it, your packaging is wrong.

Mistake: Copying formulas without substance.

Fix: Add the why. Why is it faster, cheaper, safer? Be specific.

Mistake: Vague “for everyone.”

Fix: Name your who. “Gym owners,” not “businesses.”

Mistake: Hidden dread.

Fix: Name and remove the dreaded thing (time, tech, calls, risk).

Turn clarity into conversions in your funnel today

Here are some practical applications you could do in the next 24 hours:

Run a split test with a dead-simple headline. Use language your audience is familiar with, but try cutting jargon and anything that postures you as “elite” or “bespoke” and just go straight mechanistic offer

Rewrite your warm traffic VSL to open with a more direct “here’s exactly what we do and here’s why you need it” (cold traffic needs a much stronger opener)

Send an email with similar framing as the “The 3-sentence offer that sells itself” example I gave. Make it seem like they can get an outcome in the next 10 minutes (if you’re reading this, that angle worked on you when you clicked on this Field Guide)

A “Start Here” post in your community that uses the 3-sentance breakdown you wrote, and links to book a consultation call (Oh yeah, Field Guide on internal community book-call ascension is coming soon, that’s going to be a banger)

Advanced: The 1-Page Feynman Sales Letter (for later today)

If you want to go deeper without getting fancy, build a 1-page doc (Google Doc is fine) that follows this exact narrative:

Line 1: The 10-word billboard.

Section 1: What it is (1 paragraph).

Section 2: How it works (two steps, add a simple diagram if you can).

Section 3: Why it’s better (one or two concrete advantages with a quick proof screenshot or number, or an Old Way – New Way graphic).

Section 4: Who it’s for (name the person and their current situation).

Section 5: What it costs and what happens next (one paragraph + one button to book/buy).

This “dynamic doc” style is perfect for fast iteration, showing on calls, and even potentially testing ad traffic before you overbuild a site.

If you’re not familiar with the reference, Richard Feynman is widely associated with the idea that if you can’t explain something simply, you don’t really understand it. He used this to teach physics. We use it to sell offers.

If you’re going to be lazy and not do any of the exercises, just fill this out:

Who I help:

One result they want:

One dreaded thing they hate:

What it is (1 sentence):

How it works (2 steps):

Why it’s good (1 concrete advantage):

Mechanism in a sentence:

10-word billboard:

60-second VSL opener (use the template above):

If you read this far, you get to be the first to know:

I’m going to be donig live offer teardowns inside the community. Meaning I’ll be running exercises like this on your offers, for free.

Keep your eyes peeled for that

Go crush it. Hit me if you have any questions.

– RL

# WORKSHOP CONTENT OUTLINE: YOUR SECTION
## "Fix Your Offer" - The Offer Alignment Framework for Agencies

**Duration:** 45-60 minutes  
**Format:** Teaching + Live Demo Walkthroughs  
**Goal:** Show agencies how to diagnose and fix their offer misalignments using real examples

---

## OPENING HOOK (3 minutes)

### The Problem Statement

**"Why are agencies stuck at $20K/month?"**

Not because they're bad at delivery.  
Not because they need better ads.  
Not because they need more case studies.

**It's because their offer is structurally broken.**

### The Three Symptoms

1. **Commoditization** - Competing on price with every other agency
2. **Risk Reversal** - Prospects saying "too risky" or asking for pay-per-performance
3. **Timeline Mismatch** - "I'll think about it" or "Let's wait until Q2"

### The Promise

"In the next 45 minutes, I'm going to show you the exact framework I use to audit agency offers, and I'm going to walk through three real examples where I helped agencies break through their revenue ceiling by fixing one thing: their offer architecture."

---

## SECTION 1: THE OFFER ALIGNMENT FRAMEWORK (10 minutes)

### The 5 Components

Every offer has 5 components. Most agencies only think about 2 of them.

#### 1. **NICHE** - Who are you selling to?
- Not just "eCommerce" or "B2B SaaS"
- Specific ICP: revenue range, current situation, decision maker
- **Validation question:** Is there urgent demand in this niche?

#### 2. **TRANSFORMATION** - What outcome are they buying?
- Not features ("we'll run your ads")
- Not process ("we'll optimize your campaigns")
- **The emotional + logical trigger that closes the sale**
- **Validation question:** Does the market believe you can deliver this?

#### 3. **MECHANISM** - How do you deliver it?
- **Two parts most people miss:**
  - Delivery mechanism (how you fulfill)
  - Payment mechanism (how they buy)
- **Validation question:** Does the payment structure match market risk tolerance?

#### 4. **PRICE** - What does it cost?
- Not just the number
- Structure: one-time, monthly, milestone-based?
- **Validation question:** Does the price match the perceived value and risk?

#### 5. **GUARANTEE** - How do you de-risk it?
- Explicit guarantees
- Implicit de-risking (ownership, milestones, refundable deposits)
- **Validation question:** Who absorbs the risk?

### The Diagnostic Process

**For each component, mark it as:**
- ✅ **Validated** - Market evidence confirms this works
- ⚠️ **High Risk** - Market evidence shows this will suppress conversions
- ❌ **Misaligned** - Directly conflicts with market demand

**The prescription:**
- Identify the **Strongest Validation Point** (what the market desperately wants)
- Identify the **Highest Risk Assumption** (what will kill your conversions)
- Design **The Single Most Important Fix** (one high-leverage change)

---

## SECTION 2: LIVE DEMO #1 - COLLIN (GOOGLE/YOUTUBE ADS) (12 minutes)

### The Setup

**Who:** Google/YouTube Ads agency  
**Current offer:** $2.5K-$5K/month retainers  
**Revenue:** Stuck, can't scale past current client load  

### The Diagnosis

**Walk through the 5 components on screen:**

1. ✅ **Niche:** VALIDATED
   - DTC eCommerce $2M-$20M, scaled on Meta
   - Urgent demand to diversify away from Meta dependency

2. ⚠️ **Transformation:** HIGH RISK
   - Promise: "Independent new customer acquisition channel via Google"
   - **Problem:** Market doesn't believe Google = cold acquisition
   - **Evidence from sales calls:** "Google just captures warm/brand traffic"

3. ✅ **Mechanism (Delivery):** VALIDATED
   - DFY service works fine

4. ⚠️ **Mechanism (Payment) + Price/Guarantee:** HIGH RISK
   - Monthly retainer with no cold-proof de-risking
   - **Problem:** Prospect absorbs all risk, no proof it's actually cold traffic

5. **Core Objection:** "Why not just spend more on Meta?"

### The Prescription

**The Single Most Important Fix:**

Reframe from "Google Ads Management" to **"90-Day Cold Acquisition System Install"**

**Key changes:**

| Old Positioning | New Positioning |
|----------------|-----------------|
| "We'll manage your Google Ads" | "We'll install the cold acquisition system" |
| Monthly retainer | 90-day one-time install → then retainer |
| Compared to other Google agencies | Unique category: Cold Acquisition Install |
| Success = ROAS | Success = MER/nCAC (operator language) |
| Hope it works | Cold-only proof built into deliverables |

**The Deliverables (handle the objection IN the offer):**
- Brand exclusion SOPs
- Non-brand campaign structures
- nCAC/MER reporting dashboards
- Incrementality testing framework
- Attribution setup

**The Unlock:**
- Borrow all existing agency case studies (same system, different packaging)
- Price: $4K-$6K one-time (comped toward first retainer month)
- Post-BFCM launch angle: "Did Meta dependency kill your Black Friday?"

### The Result

**Before:** Competing with every Google Ads agency on price  
**After:** Own category, higher prices, handles main objection in the offer itself

---

## SECTION 3: LIVE DEMO #2 - KRISHANT (B2B OUTBOUND) (12 minutes)

### The Setup

**Who:** B2B cold email/LinkedIn outbound agency  
**Current offer:** $2,600-$7,000 upfront pilot fees  
**Problem:** Every prospect asking for pay-per-appointment, forced to negotiate down to $500/month just to close

### The Diagnosis

**Walk through the 5 components:**

1. ❌ **Niche:** MISALIGNED
   - Targeting everyone: cleaning, solar, security, consulting
   - **Problem:** Too broad = commoditized = compared to "last agency"

2. ✅ **Transformation:** ALIGNED
   - "Qualified meetings without adding headcount"
   - Market wants this

3. ❌ **Mechanism (Payment):** MISALIGNED (CRITICAL)
   - Upfront pilot fee shifts all risk to buyer
   - **Evidence from sales calls:** "Cost is not the main factor, outlaying offer is"
   - "I'm considering someone who's pay-per-appointment"
   - **The market is TELLING YOU what they want**

4. ❌ **Price/Guarantee:** MISALIGNED
   - Pricing all over the place ($7K to $500/month)
   - No risk reversal

5. **Core Objection:** "I've been burned by agencies before, I'm not paying upfront"

### The Prescription

**Two-part fix:**

**Part 1: Positioning**
"We install the **SaaS-grade outbound operating system** inside traditional B2B service firms"

**Why this works:**
- Gets OUT of comparison ("lead gen agency")
- Creates unique category (SaaS playbook transplant)
- Implies sophistication and proven results

**Part 2: Mechanism**
Replace upfront pilot with **Guardrailed Performance Pilot**

**Structure:**
- $500 refundable deposit (covers hard costs, screens unserious buyers)
- $450 per attended qualified executive meeting
- Capped at 8-12 meetings over 30 days
- Strict ICP controls (title, geo, revenue, one per account)
- No-show replacement policy
- Ascension: Convert to $4,200/month retainer or continue pay-per-appointment

**The Insight:**
"You can't stiffarm the market. They're TELLING YOU they want pay-per-performance. Give it to them, but with guardrails that protect your unit economics."

**Language shift:**
- Stop saying "pilot" (signals you're testing if it works)
- Say "Outbound OS Install" (signals you know exactly what to install)

### The Result

**Before:** Defending upfront fees, negotiating on price, losing to pay-per-appointment competitors  
**After:** Give market what they want (performance-based) with guardrails, unique positioning eliminates comparison

---

## SECTION 4: LIVE DEMO #3 - NOAH (LOCAL SEO) (12 minutes)

### The Setup

**Who:** Local SEO agency for service businesses  
**Current offer:** $2.5K-$5K/month SEO retainers  
**Problem:** Prospects saying "Are we too premature?" and "I need to see results before committing"

### The Diagnosis

**Walk through the 5 components:**

1. ✅ **Niche:** ALIGNED
   - Local service businesses $1M-$3M+ (HVAC, medspa, detailing)
   - Strong pain: inconsistent lead flow, bad agency experiences

2. ⚠️ **Transformation:** PARTIALLY ALIGNED
   - Strong emotional resonance ("dominate your local market")
   - **Problem:** Weak financial anchoring (no ROI math, no time-to-value clarity)

3. ❌ **Mechanism:** MISALIGNED (CRITICAL)
   - Retainer-first SEO with 4-6+ month ramp
   - Requires prerequisites (reviews, GBP setup, site fixes)
   - **Problem:** "Pay for months before seeing results" + "Need to fix things first" = double bind

4. ❌ **Price/Guarantee:** MISALIGNED
   - Treating prerequisites as "upsells" creates cognitive dissonance
   - Month-to-month terms clash with long SEO ramp (invites churn before payoff)

5. **Core Objection:** "I'll never sign a contract again" + "Are we too premature to start?"

### The Prescription

**The Single Most Important Fix:**

Replace retainer-first with **"Local Dominance Sprint"** (10-12 weeks, DFY one-time)

**The Deliverables:**
- GBP creation/ownership transfer
- Full GBP optimization
- Review engine setup (templates, automation)
- Site/on-page fixes for top money pages
- Citations/NAP cleanup
- Baseline and 45-day heatmaps
- Tracking/attribution setup
- Transition/offboarding support from prior agency

**Pricing:**
- $3.5K-$5K (single location) or $5K-$8K (multi-location)
- Milestone billing: 60% kickoff / 40% completion
- **Guarantee:** "If we don't deliver documented Sprint deliverables within 12 weeks, final 40% is waived"

**Ascension Paths:**
- **Track A:** Google Ads Management (fast lead flow, 30-day ROI)
- **Track B:** SEO Authority-Build (compounding demand, 6-12 month path)

**The Insight:**
"80% of the work you do in a 6-month retainer happens in month 1 anyway. You're already doing the Sprint, you're just packaging it wrong and spreading the billing across six months, which makes the math not work for the buyer."

**The Reframe:**
"Pay once to own the engine, then pay monthly if you want us to drive it"

### The Result

**Before:** Timing objections, prerequisite blockers, contract aversion  
**After:** Finite commitment, quick wins, client owns assets, clear ascension path

---

## SECTION 5: THE UNIVERSAL PATTERNS (8 minutes)

### Pattern 1: The Retainer → Install → Retainer Model

**The problem with retainer-first:**
- Prospect absorbs all risk
- Long time to results
- Compared to other agencies
- "Hope it works" mentality

**The solution:**
- Productized installation (finite, deliverable-based)
- Client owns the assets
- Quick wins and baselines
- THEN ascend to retainer (after trust is earned)

**The math:**
Most agency work happens in first 60 days (setup, systems, baselines). Package that as a one-time install, then ongoing management becomes an easy upsell.

### Pattern 2: Language is EVERYTHING

**Bad language (increases perceived effort):**
- "Mentorship," "coaching," "we'll teach you"
- "Build your system"
- "Step-by-step guidance"
- "Pilot" (signals testing)

**Good language (decreases perceived effort):**
- "Install," "plug-and-play," "steal our system"
- "Done-for-you," "access to"
- "Operating System Install"

**The difference:**
"I'll show you how to change your oil" vs. "I'll change your oil for you"

Same backend work. Radically different perceived value.

### Pattern 3: Handle Objections IN the Offer

**Don't try to overcome objections with better sales skills.**

**Build the solution to the objection into the deliverables.**

**Examples:**
- Collin: "Google = warm traffic" → Cold-only proof mechanisms in deliverables
- Krishant: "Too risky upfront" → Refundable deposit + pay-per-meeting
- Noah: "Too premature" → Prerequisites bundled into Sprint

### Pattern 4: Stop Competing, Start Creating

**If you position as:**
- "Google Ads agency"
- "Lead gen agency"
- "SEO agency"

**You're compared to every other agency in that category.**

**Result:** Compete on price and terms.

**Solution:** Create a unique category through mechanism + positioning.

**Examples:**
- "Cold Acquisition System Install with MER/nCAC Proof"
- "SaaS-Grade Outbound OS Transplant"
- "Local Dominance Sprint"

### Pattern 5: The Market is Always Right

**When prospects repeatedly say:**
- "Can you do pay-per-performance?"
- "This feels too risky"
- "Are we too premature?"

**They're not giving objections.**

**They're telling you the offer is wrong.**

You can't overcome this with better copy or closing skills. You need a different offer structure.

---

## SECTION 6: YOUR ACTION PLAN (5 minutes)

### Step 1: Audit Your Current Offer

Run it through the 5 components:
1. Niche - Who are you selling to?
2. Transformation - What are they buying?
3. Mechanism - How do you deliver + how do they pay?
4. Price - What does it cost?
5. Guarantee - How do you de-risk it?

### Step 2: Analyze Your Sales Calls

**Closed calls:** What transformation are they actually buying?  
**DNC calls:** What's the core objection? (Not surface, but the real blocker)

### Step 3: Identify the Misalignment

Which component is misaligned with what the market is telling you?

Usually:
- Mechanism (payment structure, risk allocation)
- Transformation (market doesn't believe your promise)
- Price/Guarantee (not enough de-risking)

### Step 4: Design Your Prescription

**The single most important fix** that closes the gap.

### Step 5: Validate Before Full Launch

**72-hour positioning test:**
- One-page landing page
- Twitter/X poll
- DM 10 ICP operators for feedback

**Don't build the whole thing. Test the positioning first.**

---

## CLOSING (3 minutes)

### The Three Takeaways

1. **Your offer is the foundation.** Not your copy, not your ads, not your case studies. Fix the offer first.

2. **The market tells you what it wants.** Listen to your DNC calls. They're giving you the prescription.

3. **Retainer-first is dead for most agencies.** Install-first, then retainer. Package the first 60 days as a productized deliverable.

### The Invitation

"If you want me to audit your offer like I did for Collin, Krishant, and Noah, here's what's available..."

[Transition to ascension mechanism - exit survey, Q&A, or direct offer]

---

## SUPPORTING MATERIALS NEEDED

### Slides/Visuals

1. **The 5 Components Framework** (visual diagram)
2. **Collin's Before/After** (side-by-side comparison table)
3. **Krishant's Before/After** (side-by-side comparison table)
4. **Noah's Before/After** (side-by-side comparison table)
5. **Language Comparison Chart** (bad vs. good language)
6. **The Retainer → Install → Retainer Model** (visual flow)
7. **Action Plan Checklist** (downloadable)

### Handouts/Resources

1. **The 5-Component Offer Audit Template** (fillable worksheet)
2. **Language Swaps Cheat Sheet** (bad → good language examples)
3. **72-Hour Validation Checklist** (step-by-step guide)
4. **Sales Call Analysis Template** (how to extract insights from calls)

### Live Demo Materials

1. **Collin's actual audit report** (redacted/anonymized if needed)
2. **Krishant's actual audit report**
3. **Noah's actual audit report**
4. **Key quotes from sales calls** (VOC evidence)

---

## DELIVERY NOTES

### Pacing

- **Fast on framework** (people get frameworks quickly)
- **Slow on live demos** (this is where the value is)
- **Interactive on action plan** (get them thinking about their own offer)

### Energy

- **Confident, not salesy** (you're diagnosing, not pitching)
- **Evidence-based** (constantly reference the sales calls and market feedback)
- **Generous** (give away the methodology, hold back the implementation)

### Transitions

- **Between demos:** "See the pattern? Let's look at a completely different niche..."
- **To action plan:** "Now it's your turn. Here's exactly how to do this for your own offer..."
- **To close:** "This is the methodology. These are real examples. This works."

---

## ALIGNMENT WITH WORKSHOP PHILOSOPHY

### Anti-Guru Positioning
- ✅ Real client examples (not made-up case studies)
- ✅ Show the actual work (audit reports, call transcripts)
- ✅ Prove competence through methodology (not Miami balconies)

### Diagnostic Approach
- ✅ Help them self-diagnose their misalignment
- ✅ Exit survey routes them to appropriate solution
- ✅ Clarity over transformation (at $97 price point)

### Generous Education
- ✅ Give away the framework
- ✅ Show the live examples
- ✅ Provide actionable templates
- ✅ Still converts (Ryan Clog model)

### Collaborative Nature
- ✅ Complements Clint's sales/infrastructure content
- ✅ Sets up ascension to your offer, Michael's SaaS offer, Clint's offer
- ✅ Cross-referencing throughout ("Clint will show you the math on this...")

---

## POST-WORKSHOP ASCENSION

### Exit Survey Questions

1. "What's your current monthly revenue?"
2. "What's your current offer structure?" (retainer/one-time/hybrid)
3. "What's your biggest bottleneck right now?"
   - [ ] My offer is commoditized (competing on price)
   - [ ] My close rate is too low (risk/objections)
   - [ ] My delivery is too manual (can't scale)
   - [ ] I need to add a new revenue stream

4. "Based on what you learned, what's your next step?"
   - [ ] Fix my current offer positioning
   - [ ] Add a productized installation offer
   - [ ] Launch a new offer to a different segment
   - [ ] Get a full offer audit

### Routing Logic

**If "commoditized" + "fix positioning"** → Your offer audit service  
**If "need new revenue stream" + "SaaS"** → Michael's offer  
**If "delivery too manual" + "infrastructure"** → Clint's offer  
**If "close rate too low"** → Combination (your audit + Clint's sales)

---

## FINAL NOTES

This content is **live demo heavy**, which aligns perfectly with the workshop philosophy of "show, don't tell." You're not teaching theory - you're walking through real transformations with real clients.

The three examples cover different niches (eCommerce, B2B, local services) and different problems (transformation skepticism, risk allocation, timeline mismatch), which shows the framework is universal.

The action plan is concrete and immediately actionable (72-hour validation test), which gives them a clear next step even if they don't buy anything.

This positions you as the "offer guy" in the trio, complements Clint's "infrastructure/math guy" positioning, and sets up natural cross-referrals.

# Field Guide 03: Decommoditizing Your Offer – How to Escape the Price Comparison Death Spiral

## Intro

You're on a sales call. You've got your script ready. You watched the Jeremy Miner videos. You know your framing techniques.

Four minutes in, you realize you're not leading anything—you're being interviewed.

"What software do you use?"
"How many clients have you worked with?"
"What's your turnaround time?"
"Can you do it for less?"

You're not closing. You're defending your price.

Here's what happened: You got commoditized.

And no amount of "tonality" or "framing" or "case studies" will fix it if your offer is fundamentally positioned as a commodity.

When you read this Field Guide, you will understand exactly why your sales calls turn into interrogations, why prospects ghost after hearing your price, and why your "premium positioning" isn't working. More importantly, you'll walk away with a step-by-step process to decommoditize your offer so prospects stop comparing you to everyone else and start seeing you as the only logical choice.

You're going to learn:
- Why commoditization isn't about "being like everyone else"—it's about how the market *perceives* what you're buying them
- The exact moment in your funnel/call where commoditization happens (hint: it's earlier than you think)
- How to reframe your offer so price conversations disappear
- The "Product-ization Framework" that turns your service into something tangible they can't find elsewhere

When you're done, you'll immediately restructure your offer, rewrite your sales messaging, and watch your close rates climb—because you'll finally be selling something they actually want to buy, not just "your time."

---

## The Commoditization Trap (And Why You're Stuck In It)

Let's start with the uncomfortable truth:

**Commoditization isn't about offering the same service as everyone else. It's about the market perceiving that what they're buying from you is interchangeable with what they're buying from someone else.**

You think you're unique because:
- You have a "proprietary system"
- You've got case studies
- You position yourself as an expert
- You have a YouTube channel

But here's what your prospect sees:

"X meetings per month."
"We'll run ads to your funnel."
"We'll help you scale."
"Done-for-you lead gen."

They've heard this exact pitch from five other people this week.

So what do they do? **They price shop.**

Because if you're all offering the same thing, the only variable left is price.

### The Two Ways You Win a Commoditized Sale

If you're selling a commodity, there are only two ways you close the deal:

# Field Guide 03: Decommoditizing Your Offer – How to Escape the Price Comparison Death Spiral

## Intro

You're on a sales call. You've got your script ready. You watched the Jeremy Miner videos. You know your framing techniques.

Four minutes in, you realize you're not leading anything—you're being interviewed.

"What software do you use?"
"How many clients have you worked with?"
"What's your turnaround time?"
"Can you do it for less?"

You're not closing. You're defending your price.

Here's what happened: You got commoditized.

And no amount of "tonality" or "framing" or "case studies" will fix it if your offer is fundamentally positioned as a commodity.

When you read this Field Guide, you will understand exactly why your sales calls turn into interrogations, why prospects ghost after hearing your price, and why your "premium positioning" isn't working. More importantly, you'll walk away with a step-by-step process to decommoditize your offer so prospects stop comparing you to everyone else and start seeing you as the only logical choice.

You're going to learn:
- Why commoditization isn't about "being like everyone else"—it's about how the market *perceives* what you're buying them
- The exact moment in your funnel/call where commoditization happens (hint: it's earlier than you think)
- How to reframe your offer so price conversations disappear
- The "Product-ization Framework" that turns your service into something tangible they can't find elsewhere

When you're done, you'll immediately restructure your offer, rewrite your sales messaging, and watch your close rates climb—because you'll finally be selling something they actually want to buy, not just "your time."

---

## The Commoditization Trap (And Why You're Stuck In It)

Let's start with the uncomfortable truth:

**Commoditization isn't about offering the same service as everyone else. It's about the market perceiving that what they're buying from you is interchangeable with what they're buying from someone else.**

You think you're unique because:
- You have a "proprietary system"
- You've got case studies
- You position yourself as an expert
- You have a YouTube channel

But here's what your prospect sees:

"X meetings per month."
"We'll run ads to your funnel."
"We'll help you scale."
"Done-for-you lead gen."

They've heard this exact pitch from five other people this week.

So what do they do? **They price shop.**

Because if you're all offering the same thing, the only variable left is price.

### The Two Ways You Win a Commoditized Sale

If you're selling a commodity, there are only two ways you close the deal:

**a) You beat competition to market** – Your lead has never heard of your competitor, so they don't know they're supposed to compare

**b) Perceived price** – You SEEM cheaper, faster, or lower-risk than the alternative

That's it. Those are your only levers.

And if you're relying on either of those, you're not building a business—you're playing roulette.

---

## Where Commoditization Actually Happens

Most people think commoditization happens because "everyone's doing the same thing."

Wrong.

Commoditization happens **the moment your prospect frames what you're selling as a service, not a product.**

Here's the shift:

**Service:** "I need someone to run my ads."
**Product:** "I need the 90-Day Client Acquisition System."

**Service:** "I need a funnel built."
**Product:** "I need the Plug-and-Profit Sales Machine."

**Service:** "I need help with my offer."
**Product:** "I need the Offer Surgery Blueprint."

When they're buying a service, they're buying *your time.* And time is infinite. Every agency, freelancer, and consultant has time to sell.

When they're buying a product, they're buying *a specific outcome delivered through a specific mechanism.* And that? That's scarce.

### The "Job Interview" Sales Call

You know the call I'm talking about.

You open with your script. You try to frame. You ask discovery questions.

And within minutes, they've flipped the dynamic.

Now *they're* asking the questions:
- "What's your process?"
- "How long does it take?"
- "What tools do you use?"
- "How much does it cost?"

You're no longer selling. You're being auditioned.

**Why does this happen?**

Because they've already mentally categorized you as a service provider, not a solution provider.

They're not asking "Will this work?" They're asking "Are you worth what you're charging?"

And the second you're defending your price, you've lost.

---

## The Product-ization Framework

Here's how you fix it.

You need to turn your service into a product. Not literally (you don't need to build software), but perceptually.

**A product has:**
1. A name
2. A defined scope
3. A clear mechanism
4. A tangible deliverable
5. A specific outcome
6. A fixed timeline

Let's break it down.

### Step 1: Name Your Thing

Stop saying "I do Facebook ads" or "I help with offers."

Start saying:

"We built the 90-Day Client Acquisition System."
"I run the Offer Surgery Blueprint."
"We install the Plug-and-Profit Sales Machine."

The name does two things:
- It makes your offer *real* in their mind
- It gives them something to compare against (spoiler: no one else has your thing)

**Exercise:**

Fill in the blank:

"I built/run/install the _____________ for [who]."

The blank should be:
- Specific (not vague like "Growth System")
- Outcome-driven (what does it DO?)
- Memorable (can they repeat it to a friend?)

### Step 2: Define the Scope

A service is infinite. A product has edges.

**Service:** "We'll run ads until you hit your goal."
**Product:** "We'll build, launch, and optimize one ad funnel over 90 days."

**Service:** "We'll help you get clients."
**Product:** "We'll install a 5-page funnel, write 10 ad scripts, and train your team on follow-up."

See the difference?

The second one has boundaries. It's not "we'll keep working until you're happy." It's "here's what you get."

**Exercise:**

Write your offer as a fixed scope:

"You get [X deliverables] delivered over [Y timeframe] to achieve [Z outcome]."

### Step 3: Make the Mechanism Crystal Clear

This is where most people fail.

They say "we'll get you clients" but never explain *how.*

And when the prospect doesn't understand the mechanism, they default to price.

**Your mechanism should be:**
- Simple (2-3 steps max)
- Mechanistic (specific actions, not vague "strategies")
- Believable (not "secret sauce" bullshit)

**Example:**

"We take your best content, turn it into one simple offer, and run ads to a page that books calls. We follow up with everyone who clicks until they book. You get 5-10 calls a week without posting more."

Now they know *exactly* what you do. No mystery. No confusion.

**Exercise:**

Rewrite your mechanism in 2-3 sentences:

"We [step 1]. Then we [step 2]. You get [specific outcome] without [dreaded thing]."

### Step 4: Create a Tangible Deliverable

People need to *see* what they're buying.

This is why SaaS sells so well—there's a dashboard, a login, something concrete.

Your service needs the same.

**Examples:**

- "You get a 5-page funnel, hosted on your domain, live within 2 weeks."
- "You get 10 ad scripts, 20 email templates, and a follow-up tracker."
- "You get a 30-page Offer Surgery Report with before/after positioning."

Notice how these are all tangible. You can visualize them. You can screenshot them. You can show them to your team.

**Exercise:**

List 3-5 tangible deliverables your client will receive:

1. _____________
2. _____________
3. _____________
4. _____________
5. _____________

### Step 5: Anchor the Outcome

Your offer needs one clear, measurable outcome.

Not "we'll help you grow."

Not "we'll optimize your funnel."

**One specific result:**

- "5-10 booked calls per week"
- "30% conversion rate increase"
- "$50k in additional revenue"

The more specific, the better.

**Exercise:**

Write your one-sentence outcome:

"You will [specific, measurable result] within [timeframe]."

### Step 6: Set a Fixed Timeline

A service can drag on forever. A product has a start and end date.

**Service:** "We'll work together until you hit your goals."
**Product:** "This is a 90-day engagement. Week 1, we build. Week 2-8, we optimize. Week 9-12, we scale."

The timeline does three things:
- It creates urgency
- It sets expectations
- It makes your offer feel *finite* (and therefore valuable)

**Exercise:**

Map your offer to a timeline:

- Week 1-2: _____________
- Week 3-6: _____________
- Week 7-12: _____________

---

## Putting It All Together: The Decommoditized Offer Formula

Here's the full formula:

**"We built the [NAME] for [WHO]. You get [DELIVERABLES] over [TIMELINE] to achieve [OUTCOME] without [DREADED THING]. It works by [2-STEP MECHANISM]."**

**Example (Agency):**

"We built the 90-Day Client Acquisition System for B2B coaches. You get one funnel, 10 ad scripts, and automated follow-ups over 90 days to generate 5-10 booked calls per week without hiring a sales team. It works by turning your best content into one simple offer and running ads to a page that books calls."

**Example (Community):**

"We built the 30-Day Sprint Blueprint for community owners. You get a guided checklist, 4 live calls, and progress tracking over 30 days to help your members hit one specific win without you creating more content. It works by focusing on execution, not education—we track milestones and hold them accountable."

**Example (SaaS):**

"We built the Inbox-to-CRM Pipeline for sales teams. You get automatic data capture, email sequencing, and deal tracking over 14 days to save 10+ hours per week without manual data entry. It works by watching your inbox, filling your CRM, and sending follow-ups for you."

---

## How This Changes Your Sales Process

Once your offer is decommoditized, your sales calls change *instantly.*

Before:
- "What's your process?"
- "How much do you charge?"
- "Can you do it cheaper?"

After:
- "Tell me more about the 90-Day System."
- "How does the follow-up automation work?"
- "When can we start?"

**Why?**

Because they're no longer buying "Facebook ads." They're buying *the 90-Day Client Acquisition System.*

And no one else has that.

### The New Discovery Call Flow

Here's how your calls should flow now:

**1. Anchor the Product (30 seconds)**

"Thanks for hopping on. Just so we're on the same page—this call is about the [PRODUCT NAME]. It's designed for [WHO] who want [OUTCOME]. Sound good?"

**2. Qualify (2-3 minutes)**

"Quick questions to make sure this is a fit:
- Are you currently [doing X]?
- Have you tried [Y] before?
- What would hitting [OUTCOME] do for your business?"

**3. Explain the Mechanism (3-4 minutes)**

"Here's how it works: [2-step mechanism]. You'll get [deliverables] over [timeline]. Most clients see [result] within [timeframe]."

**4. Handle Objections (2-3 minutes)**

"Any questions about how it works?"

(Note: You're NOT defending your price. You're explaining the product.)

**5. Close (1 minute)**

"If this sounds like a fit, we can get started [timeline]. I'll send over the agreement and we'll kick off [date]. Sound good?"

---

## Real-World Examples Across Niches

### Coaches/Consultants

**Before:** "We help B2B coaches scale with ads."

**After:** "We built the 90-Day Client Acquisition System for B2B coaches. You get one funnel, 10 ad scripts, and automated follow-ups to generate 5-10 booked calls per week without hiring a sales team."

### Agency Owners

**Before:** "We do done-for-you lead gen."

**After:** "We built the Plug-and-Profit Pipeline for agencies. You get one offer page, 20 email templates, and a follow-up tracker over 30 days to turn cold leads into booked calls without manual outreach."

### Community Owners

**Before:** "I run a community for [niche]."

**After:** "We built the 30-Day Sprint Blueprint for community owners. Your members get a guided checklist, 4 live calls, and progress tracking to hit one specific win without you creating more content."

### SaaS

**Before:** "We offer workflow automation."

**After:** "We built the Inbox-to-CRM Pipeline for sales teams. You get automatic data capture, email sequencing, and deal tracking to save 10+ hours per week without manual data entry."

---

## Common Mistakes (And How to Fix Them)

### Mistake 1: You're Still Selling Time

**Fix:** Reframe your offer around deliverables, not hours.

**Before:** "We'll work with you for 90 days."
**After:** "You get X, Y, Z delivered over 90 days."

### Mistake 2: Your Name Is Generic

**Fix:** Add specificity.

**Before:** "The Growth System"
**After:** "The 90-Day Client Acquisition System"

### Mistake 3: You're Explaining Too Much

**Fix:** Simplify the mechanism to 2 steps.

**Before:** "We analyze your market, build personas, create ad copy, test audiences, optimize campaigns, and iterate."
**After:** "We turn your best content into one offer and run ads to a page that books calls."

### Mistake 4: You're Competing on Price

**Fix:** Stop talking about price until they understand the product.

If they ask about price early, redirect:

"Totally fair question—before we get there, let me make sure this is even a fit. [Ask qualifying questions.]"

---

## Homework: The Decommoditization Checklist

Here's what you're going to do in the next 24 hours:

**☐ Step 1:** Name your offer using the formula: "The [NAME] for [WHO]"

**☐ Step 2:** Write your scope: "You get [X deliverables] over [Y timeline]"

**☐ Step 3:** Simplify your mechanism: "It works by [2-step process]"

**☐ Step 4:** List 3-5 tangible deliverables

**☐ Step 5:** Define your one measurable outcome

**☐ Step 6:** Map your timeline (Week 1, Week 2, etc.)

**☐ Step 7:** Rewrite your sales call opener using the new framing

**☐ Step 8:** Update your funnel headline/VSL opener to reflect the new product name

---

## Advanced: The "Reverse Commoditization" Play

Once you've decommoditized your core offer, here's the next level:

**Create a "competitor comparison" page.**

List your offer vs. "traditional agencies" or "freelancers."

**Example:**

| Traditional Agency | The 90-Day System |
|--------------------|-------------------|
| Vague timelines | Fixed 90 days |
| Hourly billing | Flat fee |
| No clear deliverables | 10 scripts, 1 funnel, tracking |
| "We'll see what happens" | 5-10 calls/week or refund |

This reframes the entire conversation. They're no longer comparing you to other agencies—they're comparing agencies to *your product.*

---

## Final Thoughts

Commoditization isn't about being the same as everyone else.

It's about being *perceived* as the same.

And the fix isn't better positioning, case studies, or sales scripts.

It's turning your service into a product.

When you do that, price conversations disappear. Job interview calls disappear. Ghosting disappears.

Because you're no longer selling time—you're selling *a thing.*

And people will always pay more for a thing they can visualize, understand, and compare nothing else to.

Now go build your product.

– RL

For this week's Field Guide, it was based on this initial note to myself:
"Commiditization is misunderstood. If you’re offering the same thing as someone else, the ONLY way you’ll make the sale is is a) you beat competition to market (your lead literally doesn’t know who your competitor is) or b) perceived price (you SEEM cheaper than competition) This is why sales calls never go how you think. You’re reading scripts, watching Jeremy Miner videos, and then as soon as you’re on the call you don’t even get the opportunity to frame. It immediately turns into a job interview. Because they are price shopping. They KNOW you offer the same thing, likely as an agency they already worked with, they assume you’re going to get the same or worse results, so they want it to make sense. They already have numbers in their head "
I also wrote this tweet loosely about this: "Commoditization is completely misunderstood People know it’s “bad” to be commoditized. But what about your business is actually commoditized? Example I see all the time: Agency offers the typical “X-Y meetings per month.” They lean on case studies, testimonials, social proof. YouTube videos, positioning as an expert, etc. everything seems okay enough on paper Then when they get on sales calls, they expect to lead the discovery process, use some framing techniques they learned from their mastermind, and 4 minutes in it turns into a job interview. The prospect is only talking about price, logistics, what software you use, what results you’ve gotten Because you’re not selling A THING. You’re offering a service. It’s closer to a job than a business. Them hearing “X meetings per month” is no different than hearing a “I’m hungry and want to work” in a job application. Everyone says the same thing, so it doesn’t actually resonate as an outcome, but just as part of the script everyone reads So they only explore price. They assume you’re the exact same as all the other agencies they’ve seen or been pitched by, so they want it to “make sense for their business,” which means price What are they BUYING? There are no sales techniques or “unique mechanism” that can overpower your lack of understanding what the prospect is getting for their money, that isn’t just your “time” or “service” We’ll fix it"

I have a community called WeBuildYourOffer. A free community for coaches, consultants, and community owners who want offers that convert. We run teardowns, rebuilds, and publications that help you build offers that actually sell.
What you sell is fine. How you sell it isn’t.

Every week, I do a "Field Guide" – it's basically a rundown of something related to the business I teach. Offers, funnels, marketing, sales, mindset, etc

The goal is for me to demonstrate techniques LIVE on my audience. Teaching upsells while upselling them. Teaching funnel flows on new products I launch

Uploaded in "Guide Idea" I will provide information on the Field Guide I want to create this week. You will reference:

• "Knowledge Base" which is a swipe/dump of all my business ideas, content I have posted on business etc. so you can understand my methodoligies, opinions, skills, how I look at everything in this business landscape 
• "Previous Twitter Content" which, similar to the Knowledge Base, will give you a good understanding of my philosophy
• "Previous Field Guides" which gives you an understanding of how the Field Guides end up

You will then create a full Field Guide. It should be long, detailed, it should include all the information the reader would need to immeditaly apply it and see instant results in their business. It will have a brief into, written in my style, about what it is, why it's important, and the outcome the reader is about to have after reading (future pacing, not if they read it, WHEN they read it XYZ benefit/transformation will occur). Then the guide itself, which should be format for easy reading, comprehension and application. Then, write an "announcment" that I will post into my announcment channel revealing this week's field guide

  REQUIRED STRUCTURE:
  1. The Problem (What most people get wrong)
  2. The Example (Specific case study or breakdown)
  3. The Breakdown (3-5 key insights with explanations)
  4. The Lesson (Main takeaway tied to methodology)
  5. The Application (How to apply this to their business)

  Create a detailed outline with:
  - Hook/thesis statement
  - Bullet points for each section
  - Specific examples to include
  - Key quotes or one-liners
  - Where to add the WBYO CTA

  Keep Riley's voice: direct, specific, no fluff.

# Field Guide 03: Decommoditizing Your Offer – How to Escape the Price Comparison Death Spiral

## Intro

You're on a sales call. You've got your script ready. You watched the Jeremy Miner videos. You know your framing techniques.

Four minutes in, you realize you're not leading anything—you're being interviewed.

"What software do you use?"
"How many clients have you worked with?"
"What's your turnaround time?"
"Can you do it for less?"

You're not closing. You're defending your price.

Here's what happened: You got commoditized.

And no amount of "tonality" or "framing" or "case studies" will fix it if your offer is fundamentally positioned as a commodity.

# Master Positioning Document: The Offer Desk

**Author:** Manus AI
**Date:** November 18, 2025

## 1. Core Thesis & Guiding Philosophy

The fundamental principle of this business is that **most offers fail because they are built on mimetic imitation, not logical validation.** Founders, coaches, and agency owners are trapped in a cycle of copying what *appears* to be working for others, resulting in offers that are misaligned with what their customers actually want and need. This creates a fundamental capital efficiency problem that no amount of slick copywriting or ad spend can solve.

Our core philosophy is the antidote to this "mimetic trap." We apply a rigorous, engineering-based approach to offer creation, inspired by the frameworks of Nick Kozmin and the philosophical insights of Rene Girard. We believe that a truly **irrefutable offer** is not "created" but **validated** through a scientific process.

> **Our Mission:** To replace mimetic guesswork with logical certainty, empowering businesses to build offers so compelling they sell themselves.

## 2. Brand Identity & Market Positioning

### Brand Identity: The Offer Engineer

We are not copywriters, marketers, or funnel builders in the traditional sense. We are **Offer Engineers**. Our brand is built on a foundation of intellectual rigor, scientific methodology, and a contrarian perspective on the online business landscape.

| Brand Attribute | Description |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Intellectual & Analytical** | Our content and communication are rooted in deep thinking, frameworks, and first principles. We don't just share tactics; we deconstruct the underlying mechanics of why things work. |
| **Provocative & Contrarian** | We challenge the prevailing narratives in the "make money online" space. We are not afraid to call out flawed models and expose the mimetic traps that ensnare most entrepreneurs. |
| **Authentic & Transparent** | We are practitioners, not just theorists. We openly share our own processes, successes, and failures, using our own business as a live case study. |
| **Mechanistic & Results-Oriented** | We focus on the tangible, mechanical flaws in a business and provide clear, actionable steps to fix them. Our value is measured in the direct impact on our clients' revenue and capital efficiency. |

### Market Positioning: The Anti-Guru

In a market saturated with "gurus" selling recycled information and surface-level tactics, we position ourselves as the **anti-guru**. We are the trusted advisor for the discerning founder who is tired of the hype and hungry for a more intelligent, first-principles approach to growth.

We are not for everyone. We are for the operators who recognize that the foundation of their business is broken and are willing to do the hard, intellectual work to fix it.

## 3. Target Audience & Ideal Customer Profile

Our ideal client is a sophisticated founder or operator who has achieved a degree of success but has hit a revenue ceiling. They are frustrated, and they suspect the problem is deeper than just their marketing or sales tactics.

| Tier | Ideal Customer Profile |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Tier 1: Offer Alignment Audit** | The established coach, consultant, or agency owner with an existing offer that is underperforming. They have sales call recordings and marketing materials to be audited. |
| **Tier 2: Offer Launch Blueprint** | The successful freelancer or service provider who wants to productize their expertise and launch a scalable offer (e.g., a course or coaching program). They have a strong idea but no existing assets. |
| **Tier 3: Growth Operator Partnership** | The high-potential founder (like Joe McGrath) or established business that needs a full, end-to-end launch of a new offer or business line. They have a unique asset (like a strong personal brand or a valuable IP) and are looking for a strategic partner to help them monetize it. |

## 4. The Tiered Offer Architecture

Our services are structured as a clear ascension path, designed to meet clients where they are and provide the appropriate level of support.

| Tier | Service | Price Point | Core Deliverable |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **1** | **Offer Alignment Audit** | $497 - $997 | A comprehensive audit report and a 30-minute implementation call, diagnosing the flaws in an existing offer and providing a clear plan to fix them. |
| **2** | **Offer Launch Blueprint** | $2,500 - $5,000 | A complete, validated offer built from scratch, including the niche, transformation, price, and mechanism, delivered as a strategic blueprint. |
| **3** | **Growth Operator Partnership** | $15,000 - $50,000+ | A full-stack, done-for-you launch of a new offer, including the funnel, CRM, copy, and launch management. |

## 5. Strategic Growth Levers

Our growth will be driven by a combination of content, community, and strategic partnerships.

| Growth Lever | Description |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Content as a Product** | We will create high-value, in-depth content (like the "Field Guides") that demonstrates our expertise and serves as a lead magnet for our free community. |
| **Community as a Funnel** | The free community will be the central hub of our ecosystem. We will use a quiz funnel to segment new members and ascend them to the appropriate offer. |
| **Partnerships & Affiliates** | We will actively pursue strategic partnerships with other high-profile players in the space (like Andrew from ClickFunnels) to generate high-quality leads and expand our reach. |
| **Productized Consulting** | We will continue to productize our expertise, creating scalable, low-fulfillment offers (like the $497 audit) that can be delivered efficiently. |
| **High-Ticket as the North Star** | The Growth Operator Partnership will be our flagship service, allowing us to work with high-potential clients on a deeper level and generate significant case studies. |
